title: The Sentence Nobody Corrected Becomes the Success Metric
description: An unrealistic expectation stated in a kickoff meeting and left unaddressed doesn't go away — it quietly becomes the standard the whole engagement gets judged against.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when a client statement sets an unscoped, unverified success metric for an engagement
Distinguish what's knowable at kickoff from what isn't, and communicate that distinction to a non-technical client

contentSections.body: In a kickoff call, a client says, 'Once this AI system is live, we're planning to let go of three of our five data-entry staff next quarter.' You haven't scoped the project yet. You don't know if the system can handle the edge cases those three people currently catch, or how long it'll take to reach a reliable accuracy rate on this client's specific data. Saying nothing and moving on to the technical agenda means this exact sentence becomes the client's success metric — and if reality doesn't match it in three months, the project reads as a failure regardless of what the technology actually achieved.

The specific consulting skill here isn't technical — it's naming the expectation gap out loud, in the room, before it becomes silent scope. That means separating what's actually knowable at kickoff (this system can plausibly handle routine cases based on early testing) from what isn't (a specific headcount and a specific date), and being explicit that a headcount decision shouldn't be made on a pre-scoping guess.

Avoiding this conversation because it's uncomfortable is exactly how 'we brought in an AI consultant and it didn't deliver' narratives start. Usually the technology performed reasonably — the actual failure was an expectation nobody corrected early enough, which then hardened into the standard everyone judged the project against.

contentSections.scenario: Kickoff call. Client states a specific headcount reduction and a specific quarter, before any scoping, testing, or accuracy benchmarking has happened on their actual data.
contentSections.question: Why is staying silent on this statement a real risk to the engagement, independent of how well the technology eventually performs?

options.label: An unaddressed expectation stated this early tends to become the standard the engagement gets judged against later, whether or not it was ever realistic
Clients are generally wrong about what AI can do, so their expectations should always be corrected
This isn't actually a risk — the technical work will speak for itself regardless of what was said in the kickoff

feedback.unaddressed-becomes-metric: Correct. Nothing about staying silent makes the statement go away — it sits there as the implicit success criterion the client will use to judge the engagement, whether or not anyone ever agreed it was realistic. Naming the gap early gives both sides a chance to set a criterion that's actually connected to what scoping and testing show is achievable.
feedback.client-is-always-wrong: The point isn't that the client's expectation is necessarily wrong — it might turn out to be achievable. The point is that nobody knows yet, at kickoff, before scoping, and treating an unverified guess as a confirmed plan is the actual problem, regardless of which direction it turns out to be wrong in.
feedback.not-actually-risk: Good technical work doesn't retroactively change what the client was told to expect at kickoff. If the stated headcount reduction doesn't happen on the stated timeline, the engagement reads as a failure by the client's own stated metric, even if the system performs well by every other measure.

contentSections.mechanism: In consulting engagements, whatever specific, measurable claim goes unchallenged early tends to become the implicit definition of success later, regardless of whether it was ever scoped or verified. Naming the gap between what's known and what's assumed, at the point it's said, is how a consultant prevents an unscoped guess from becoming the project's judgment criterion.

contentSections.scenario:
Still in the kickoff call. To correct the expectation without sounding obstructive, you have to be precise about the line you're drawing — what is already known, versus what only scoping and testing can answer.

Getting this line wrong in either direction costs you. Claim too little is knowable and you sound evasive. Claim too much and you've made a second unverified promise.
contentSections.question: Select every item that is genuinely knowable at this kickoff, before any scoping or testing.

items.label: What the five data-entry staff do today, step by step
Which kinds of unusual cases staff currently catch by hand
That the client's goal for this project is reducing headcount
The accuracy the system will reach on this client's own records
That three of the five roles can be removed
That the system will be reliable enough by next quarter

explanation.current-process: Knowable — by asking, in this call. It costs nothing and it's the ground everything else gets built on. If the client can't describe the current process step by step, that itself is a finding worth naming.
explanation.what-they-catch: Knowable, and it's the question most worth asking here. The cases staff catch by hand are exactly the ones a system will have to handle or escalate, and they're usually invisible in any process document.
explanation.client-intent: Knowable — the client just said it. Naming it back as a goal rather than a plan is what lets you engage with it honestly instead of stepping around it.
explanation.accuracy-on-data: Not knowable yet. Accuracy on this client's records depends on this client's records, and nobody has looked at them. Benchmarks from other projects describe other data.
explanation.three-of-five: Not knowable — this is the assumption doing the most damage, because it's specific enough to sound like a decision that has already been made. It depends on accuracy, on which cases still need escalating, and on how much of what those three people do is the data entry itself.
explanation.next-quarter: Not knowable. A date can be planned toward, but stating it at kickoff as a fact makes it the deadline the engagement gets judged against, before anyone has seen the work it depends on.

contentSections.synthesis: The knowable items are all descriptions of the present that you can get by asking questions in the room. The unknowable ones are all predictions about the system's future behaviour on data nobody has examined. That's the line, and it's a line you can state to a non-technical client without any technical vocabulary: we can describe what happens today, and we can't yet predict what the system will do on your records until we've run it on them.

contentSections.question: The client has just said they plan to cut three of five roles next quarter. Put your response in the order that corrects the expectation without shutting the conversation down.
steps: Say the statement back, so both sides know it's now on the record
Separate what's known today from what the plan assumes
Name the specific things scoping and testing still have to answer
Ask that the headcount decision wait until those answers exist
Agree a success criterion that can be checked before the headcount date
contentSections.explanation: Repeating the statement back comes first because it makes the expectation explicit rather than something you're inferring, and it gives the client a chance to soften it themselves. Separating known from assumed comes before naming open questions, because otherwise the open questions read as a list of objections rather than as work. The ask about timing lands only after the client can see what it depends on. The last step is the one that turns the correction into something useful — without a replacement criterion, you've removed the client's measure of success and given them nothing, which is how this conversation ends up feeling like an excuse being set up in advance.

contentSections.body: Much of the actual value in AI consulting is catching and correcting expectation gaps before they harden into someone's success metric — not just doing good technical work. The uncomfortable correction in the kickoff room is cheaper than the failed-project narrative three months later.

title: '95% Accuracy' Isn't One Number — and the Difference Can Be the Whole Engagement
description: A single accuracy target hides two very different failure modes — missing a real risk versus flagging a safe case — and which one matters more depends entirely on what's actually at stake if the model is wrong.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish precision from recall as measures of a model's errors, not just its overall accuracy
Determine which error type (false positive or false negative) matters more given the real-world cost of each in a specific use case

contentSections.body: A client wants an AI system to flag risky clauses in legal contracts before a lawyer reviews them, and insists on "95% accuracy" as the success target, citing an industry benchmark. The process being automated is contract review, where missing a single liability clause can have real legal consequences for the client. "95% accuracy" sounds like a clear, reasonable bar — but it's actually hiding the one question that matters most for this specific use case.

contentSections.scenario:
The model reads a supplier agreement and makes two mistakes on it.

Mistake one: it marks a payment-terms clause as risky. The lawyer reads it and judges it routine.

Mistake two: further down the same contract there's a liability clause the model doesn't mark at all. Nobody looks at it, and the contract gets signed.
contentSections.question: Both count as one error against the accuracy score. Which one is more expensive to this client?

options.label: The liability clause the model didn't mark
The routine clause the model marked as risky
The same — each is one error

feedback.missed-liability: Correct. The two mistakes cost wildly different amounts. The unnecessary flag costs a lawyer a few minutes reading a paragraph and moving on. The missed liability clause reaches a signed contract with nobody having read it, and the cost of that is whatever the clause turns out to say.
feedback.flagged-routine: This one is real, and at volume a stream of unnecessary flags does have a cost — it makes the tool tiring to use and easier to start ignoring. But per mistake it's minutes of a lawyer's attention, against a liability clause that made it into a signed contract unread.
feedback.same-cost: They count the same in the accuracy score, which is exactly the problem being pointed at here. In the process itself they don't: one costs a few minutes of reading, the other reaches a signed contract with nobody having seen it.

contentSections.concept: These two mistakes have names. A **false positive** is the model flagging something that turns out to be fine. A **false negative** is the model missing something real. A single accuracy figure adds them together as if they were interchangeable. In any process where one of them costs far more than the other, that addition is where the important information gets lost.

contentSections.body:
"Accuracy" as a single number blends together two genuinely different kinds of mistakes a model can make:

- **False negatives**: the model misses something real — here, a risky clause that actually exists in the contract and doesn't get flagged.
- **False positives**: the model flags something that isn't actually a problem — a clause gets marked risky when a lawyer would judge it fine.

A model can hit 95% overall accuracy by being excellent at avoiding false positives while still missing a meaningful share of real risks, or the reverse — flagging everything remotely questionable and burying the lawyer in noise while still technically clearing 95% because most clauses in a typical contract are unremarkable. The two error profiles produce the identical headline number and are not remotely equivalent in a liability-sensitive process.

The consulting judgment call is: **which error is more expensive here?** In contract review, missing a real risk (false negative) usually costs far more than over-flagging a safe clause (false positive) — a lawyer re-reading one extra paragraph is cheap; an unflagged liability clause reaching a signed contract is not. That means the target shouldn't be "95% accuracy" in the abstract — it should be a recall target (catch nearly everything real) even if it costs some precision (more false alarms for the lawyer to dismiss).

contentSections.scenario:
The client originally set '95% accuracy' as the target for the contract-review model, before anyone broke that number down further. Two configurations were then tested against real contracts:

Configuration A: catches 99% of real risky clauses (recall), but also flags 15% of safe clauses as risky (lawyer reviews some unnecessary flags).
Configuration B: catches 85% of real risky clauses (recall), and only flags 3% of safe clauses as risky (fewer false alarms, but more real risks slip through unflagged).

Given that missing a real liability clause is far more costly than a lawyer dismissing an unnecessary flag: which facts below actually support recommending Configuration A over Configuration B?
contentSections.question: Select every piece of evidence that genuinely supports recommending Configuration A.

items.label: Configuration A catches 99% of real risky clauses versus 85% for Configuration B
In this use case, a lawyer dismissing an unnecessary flag costs far less than a real liability clause slipping through unflagged
The client originally pitched '95% accuracy' as the target for both configurations, before this precision/recall breakdown was run
Configuration A produces fewer false alarms than Configuration B

explanation.higher-recall: Applicable. Recall — the share of real risky clauses actually caught — is the metric that matters most given the cost asymmetry, and Configuration A's 99% substantially beats Configuration B's 85%.
explanation.asymmetric-cost: Applicable. This is the actual reasoning that should drive the recommendation: when a missed risk is far more expensive than a false alarm, the choice should favor whichever configuration catches more real risks, even at the cost of more false alarms.
explanation.same-headline-accuracy: Not applicable — that both configurations were pitched against the same 95% target is what made the headline number the client anchored on in the first place. It's evidence the original framing was too coarse to distinguish the two options, not evidence for choosing either one; the actual choice depends on the recall/precision breakdown, not on which one hits the original target number.
explanation.config-a-fewer-false-alarms: Not applicable, and backwards — Configuration A actually produces *more* false alarms than Configuration B (15% versus 3%). That's the real tradeoff being accepted, not a point in A's favor.

contentSections.synthesis: The right call is Configuration A, and the reasoning that gets there is recall plus cost asymmetry — not the shared headline accuracy number, and not false-alarm rate in isolation. A lawyer spending a few extra minutes dismissing an unnecessary flag is a minor cost; a real liability clause reaching a signed contract unflagged is a serious one. The consulting skill is identifying which error costs more in this specific process, then choosing the configuration that minimizes the expensive error — not defaulting to whichever option has the higher accuracy number or the lower false-alarm rate in isolation.

contentSections.code:
Acceptance criteria — contract risk model (client's draft)

1. Model reaches 95% accuracy on a test set of 500 clauses.
2. Test set is drawn to reflect a typical contract mix.
3. Sign-off when criterion 1 is met.
contentSections.question: Which line lets a model pass sign-off while still missing a meaningful share of real risky clauses?

options.label: Line 1 — a single accuracy figure with no separate recall requirement
Line 1 — 500 clauses is too small a test set
Line 2 — the test set reflects a typical contract mix

feedback.single-accuracy: Correct. One accuracy number can be produced by two models with completely different error profiles, and these criteria never ask which one was delivered. Configuration B from the previous exercise — catching 85% of real risky clauses — could clear a 95% accuracy bar comfortably, because most clauses in a contract are unremarkable and it gets those right. The fix is a stated recall floor alongside the accuracy figure.
feedback.test-set-size: Sample size isn't what's broken here. A test set of 5,000 clauses scored the same way would report the same blended number and hide the same tradeoff. More data measured on the wrong axis doesn't help.
feedback.typical-mix: Line 2 is doing the right thing on its own — a representative mix is what makes the test realistic. It interacts badly with line 1 though: in a typical contract most clauses are unremarkable, so a blended accuracy score is dominated by them and barely moves when the model misses risky ones. The answer isn't to skew the test set. It's to score the risky clauses separately.

contentSections.flawExplanation: These criteria are specific, measurable, and written down, which is why they read as rigorous — and they still can't distinguish a model that catches nearly every real risk from one that misses roughly one in seven. Acceptance criteria for a risk-sensitive process have to name the expensive error directly: what share of real risky clauses must be caught, measured on those clauses alone. Overall accuracy sits underneath that number, not in place of it.

contentSections.body: "Accuracy" is not a single, sufficient success metric for a risk-sensitive process — it hides the tradeoff between missing real problems and raising false alarms. The consultant's job is surfacing that tradeoff explicitly and asking which error costs more given what's actually at stake, not accepting a client's single accuracy number at face value.

title: The enquiry that means five different projects
description: A one-sentence enquiry names a feeling, not a task — the first job is enumerating the distinct plausible projects it could mean and asking the questions that tell them apart, before proposing any of them.

learningObjectives.text: Enumerate the distinct plausible projects hiding inside a vague AI enquiry before proposing any of them
Ask follow-up questions that actually disambiguate which project a client means, rather than ones that are merely interesting

contentSections.body: Priya Chandra, director of operations at Corrigan Tax & Advisory, a 45-person regional accounting firm, emails: “We want AI to help with tax season — everyone's underwater by March and we think there's something here.” That's the entire enquiry. No process description, no named bottleneck, no date. Before writing back with anything that sounds like a proposal, that one sentence needs to be taken apart — it could plausibly mean five different pieces of work, each with a different scope, timeline, and price.

A vague enquiry names a feeling, not a task. “Underwater by March” could point at any of: (1) **client document intake** — the scanned W-2s, 1099s, and receipts that arrive by email and portal and have to be sorted and entered; (2) **first-pass return drafting** — a senior reviewer building every return from scratch instead of checking a draft; (3) **client status-update emails** — “is my return done yet” questions eating staff time; (4) **staffing and capacity planning** — knowing which weeks will crush the team before they hit; (5) an **internal knowledge base** — junior staff repeatedly asking seniors questions that are already answered somewhere, if anyone could find it.

Proposing anything before separating these is a bet, not a scope. Each candidate has a different build, a different price, and a different definition of done — and Corrigan may need one, several, or something not on this list at all. The first job isn't picking the right one from memory; it's asking the questions that let Priya tell you.

contentSections.scenario: You reply to Priya asking her to describe the March crunch in her own words. She writes back: “Half our new hires spend their first two weeks just learning where things are filed for each client — which forms this client always needs, which ones this partner handles differently.”
contentSections.question: Which of the five candidate projects does this specific sentence point at?

options.label: Client document intake
An internal knowledge base
First-pass return drafting
Client status-update emails

feedback.intake: This is about staff finding institutional knowledge, not about incoming client paperwork — nothing in the sentence describes documents arriving from clients.
feedback.kb: Correct. “Learning where things are filed” and “which forms this partner handles differently” describes information that exists somewhere in Corrigan's institutional memory but isn't accessible to someone new — the definition of a knowledge-access problem, not a document-processing or drafting one.
feedback.drafting: Drafting is about producing the return itself. This sentence is about staff finding out how to do that correctly for a given client, which happens before any drafting starts.
feedback.status: Status emails are client-facing; this sentence describes an internal staff problem with no client involved at all.

contentSections.concept: The same vague enquiry can hide several genuinely distinct projects, and a client's own words — not the consultant's assumptions — tell you which one a specific complaint actually points at. Ask, don't guess.

contentSections.scenario: You're drafting your reply to Priya. You want to ask enough to tell the five candidates apart without turning the email into a 40-minute homework assignment before she's even hired you.
contentSections.question: Select every question that would actually help you tell which candidate project Corrigan needs.

items.label: What specifically happens in the two weeks before a return goes out the door, step by step?
What's the one moment last tax season where something almost went wrong, or a deadline was almost missed?
Which of these problems costs the firm the most in staff overtime hours right now?
How many tax returns did Corrigan file in total last year?
Would Corrigan prefer a cloud-based or on-premise system?

explanation.step-by-step: Applicable. A walk-through of the actual sequence of work surfaces which of the five candidates the real bottleneck sits in — you can't tell from a feeling, but you can usually tell from a described sequence of actions.
explanation.near-miss: Applicable. A specific near-miss is concrete in a way “we're underwater” isn't — it names an actual moment, which usually names an actual candidate project.
explanation.overtime-cost: Applicable. If several of the five are real problems, this is what tells you which one to scope first — the one actually costing money and hours, not the one that's most annoying to talk about.
explanation.total-returns: Not applicable at this stage. Volume matters later for pricing and tooling, but it doesn't distinguish which of the five projects Corrigan actually needs.
explanation.cloud-onprem: Not applicable yet, and premature — this is a tool question, and no project has even been chosen. Asking it now signals you've already jumped to a solution.

contentSections.synthesis: The questions that disambiguate ask for a specific sequence, a specific moment, or a specific cost — anything that turns a feeling into a described fact. Questions about volume or tooling are real questions, but they belong after a candidate project is chosen, not before.

contentSections.body: A one-sentence enquiry is a symptom, not a spec — enumerate the plausible distinct projects it could mean, then ask the questions that tell them apart, before proposing any of them.

title: Fixed scope, fixed price, and where each one bites
description: Fixed price, time-and-materials, and hybrid structures each move the same risk to a different place — knowing where a pricing model bites before signing beats discovering it mid-engagement.

learningObjectives.text: Identify where fixed-price, time-and-materials, and hybrid pricing structures each place risk
Convert a vague need into a fixed deliverable bounded by an explicit, priced discovery phase

contentSections.title: Three structures, three places the risk lands

contentSections.body: Priya's follow-up answers narrow it down: the real March crunch is document intake — clients email and upload W-2s, 1099s, and receipts in every format imaginable, and staff manually re-key them into the firm's tax software, closest to the deadline, under the most time pressure. Now comes the pricing conversation, and Denise Marsh, the managing partner, asks the question every client asks: “so what does this cost, and how do we know it won't balloon?”

Three structures answer that question differently, and each moves the same underlying risk — that the work turns out to be bigger or messier than anyone guessed — to a different party.

**Fixed scope, fixed price** bites the consultant when the client's document formats turn out messier than assumed: more broker-style variance in receipt formats, more edge cases, more re-work — all absorbed at the quoted price, or renegotiated mid-engagement in an awkward change-order conversation the client didn't expect.

**Time-and-materials (T&M)** bites the client: hours are billed as worked, which is fair when the work is genuinely unpredictable, but it means the client is carrying open-ended budget risk and has to trust that hours billed map to hours actually needed — trust that erodes fast if the number keeps climbing without visible cause.

**Hybrid** — a fixed, priced discovery phase followed by a fixed price for the now-bounded build — reduces both risks but doesn't eliminate either: it shifts the fixed-price risk onto how well the discovery phase actually characterized the messiness, and shifts the T&M risk onto a bounded number of days instead of an open-ended one.

contentSections.problem: Convert Corrigan's vague “help with document intake” into a priced structure, given that nobody yet knows how many distinct document formats Corrigan's clients actually send.

steps.label: Name the unknown that makes fixed price risky right now
steps.work: Nobody has looked at Corrigan's actual incoming documents yet — the range of formats (scanned PDFs, phone photos, spreadsheets, portal uploads) is unknown, and that range is exactly what determines how hard the extraction step is.
steps.why: Pricing a fixed build before this is known means guessing at the hardest part of the job and eating the difference if the guess is wrong — the same trap a fixed bid on an undiagnosed problem always sets.

steps.label: Bound the unknown with a priced discovery phase
steps.work: Propose a fixed-price, one-week discovery phase: pull 40–60 of Corrigan's own real client documents from the last filing season, categorize the formats and edge cases actually present, and produce a written format inventory.
steps.why: A discovery phase converts an unknown into a known, on a small, bounded budget — both sides pay a small, fixed amount to find out what the real range looks like, instead of one side absorbing the risk of guessing.

steps.label: Price the build against the now-known range
steps.work: With the format inventory in hand, quote a fixed price for the extraction pipeline, scoped explicitly to the document types the inventory found — with a stated rate for adding a format discovered later, rather than an open promise to handle “anything.”
steps.why: The build's fixed price is now grounded in an actual inventory instead of an assumption, and the stated per-format rate for later additions keeps a genuinely new edge case from becoming a free scope-creep argument.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. Corrigan also mentions, almost as an aside, wanting the first-pass return drafting problem solved — but nobody has looked at how much return-to-return variation there actually is in Corrigan's client mix. Price this the same way.

blanks.prompt: What's the unknown that makes fixed price risky here?
blanks.answer: How much genuine variation exists across Corrigan's actual returns — individual filers versus small-business returns versus anything with multiple schedules — which determines how hard first-pass drafting actually is
accept: the real range of return complexity/variation across Corrigan's client mix is unknown
blanks.why: Same shape as the intake case: the thing that determines difficulty (variation) hasn't been measured, so a fixed price right now would be a guess, not a quote.

blanks.prompt: What would a bounded discovery phase for this look like?
blanks.answer: A fixed-price, short discovery pass through a sample of last year's returns, categorized by complexity, producing a written breakdown of how many fall into each complexity tier
accept: sample last year's returns, categorize by complexity tier, produce a written inventory
blanks.why: The discovery phase's job is always the same: turn an unmeasured range into a written, categorized inventory, on a small fixed budget both sides agree to upfront.

blanks.prompt: How should the build then be priced?
blanks.answer: Fixed price for the complexity tiers the discovery phase actually found, with a separate, stated rate for a tier or return type discovered later that wasn't in the sample
accept: fixed price scoped to the discovered tiers, stated add-on rate for anything found later
blanks.why: Grounding the fixed price in the inventory, and pricing genuinely new discoveries separately, is what keeps the fixed price honest instead of becoming a silent absorption point for surprises.

faded.procedure: When a fixed price is being asked for on an unmeasured range, don't guess and don't default to open-ended T&M either — propose a small, fixed-price discovery phase that turns the unknown into a written inventory, then price the build against what the inventory actually found, with a stated rate for anything discovered later.

contentSections.title: Reading a pricing structure for where it bites

contentSections.code:
Draft proposal to Corrigan (junior colleague's version):

“We will build a complete document-intake and extraction pipeline for Corrigan Tax & Advisory, handling all client document types, for a fixed price of $18,000, delivered in six weeks.”
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in quoting this today, before anything else has happened?

options.label: “All client document types” is an unbounded promise made before anyone has looked at what Corrigan's document types actually are — the fixed price is anchored to an unknown range
$18,000 is simply too low a number for this kind of work
Six weeks is too short a timeline for any AI project

feedback.unbounded-scope: Correct. The flaw isn't the number or the date — it's that “all client document types” was priced before anyone measured what that range actually contains. If Corrigan's clients turn out to send handwritten receipts and photographed mileage logs, that fixed price now has to absorb work nobody scoped.
feedback.price-too-low: There's no way to know whether $18,000 is too low, too high, or right — that's exactly the problem. A price attached to an unmeasured scope isn't wrong because of the number; it's wrong because the number has nothing real underneath it.
feedback.timeline-too-short: Same issue — there's no way to judge whether six weeks is realistic without knowing what the actual document range looks like first. The timeline is exposed to the same unmeasured risk as the price.

contentSections.flawExplanation: “All client document types” reads as thorough, but it's a fixed commitment against an unknown quantity. The fix isn't a lower price or a longer timeline — it's not quoting a fixed price against an unmeasured range at all. A discovery phase converts “all document types” into a specific, counted list before any fixed number gets attached to it.

contentSections.body: Every pricing structure moves the same risk somewhere — fixed price to the consultant, T&M to the client, hybrid to how well discovery bounded the unknown. Name where it lands before signing, not after.

title: Pricing for outcome without pricing yourself into a hole
description: Outcome-based pricing sounds like it aligns everyone's incentives — until attribution, measurement, and factors outside the consultant's control turn a percentage-of-savings deal into an argument nobody can win.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the attribution and measurement problems that make naive outcome-based pricing risky
Design a bounded outcome-linked pricing structure with a named baseline, metric, and measurement window

contentSections.title: The pitch that sounds fair and isn't

contentSections.body: Denise Marsh likes the discovery-phase idea, then floats something else: “Honestly, why don't we just pay you a percentage of what this actually saves us in staff hours? That way we're not paying for something that doesn't work.” It sounds fair — aligned incentives, no risk to the client, payment tied to real value. It's also a pricing structure that can quietly cost the consultant far more than a fixed fee ever would, for reasons that have nothing to do with how well the work is done.

Outcome pricing has a real appeal: it removes the client's fear of paying for something that doesn't deliver. It also has three specific failure points worth naming before agreeing to it.

**Attribution.** If Corrigan also hires two new staff members mid-season, or tax law changes add complexity to a chunk of returns, staff hours might not drop the way the pipeline alone would have produced — and now there's a dispute about how much of any change is even attributable to the work.

**Measurement.** “Staff hours saved” has to be measured against something — whose timesheets, over what period, compared to what baseline — and if that wasn't nailed down before the work started, the number becomes whatever each side wants it to be.

**Factors outside the consultant's control.** Walt Sorensen, the senior reviewer, might simply keep double-checking everything by hand out of habit, regardless of how good the extraction is — which would suppress the very savings the fee depends on, for a reason that has nothing to do with the consultant's work.

contentSections.scenario: A different consultant took a 20%-of-savings deal with a similar firm last year. Six months in, the firm's staff-hour numbers barely moved, and the consultant was paid almost nothing — even though the extraction pipeline itself tested well and Corrigan's own reviewers privately said it was working.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely mechanism behind the fee not materializing, given the pipeline tested well?

options.label: Staff kept working the old, familiar way instead of adopting the new pipeline's output, so the hours the tool saved never showed up in anyone's timesheet
The pipeline was actually broken in production despite testing well beforehand
The firm deliberately under-reported hours to avoid paying the fee

feedback.adoption-gap: Correct. A tool that tests well and is available for use isn't the same as a tool that's actually been adopted into daily habits — and outcome pricing is exposed to that adoption gap even when the technical work is genuinely good, because the fee depends on a behavior change the consultant doesn't fully control.
feedback.tool-actually-broken: The scenario states the pipeline tested well and reviewers privately said it was working — the technical quality isn't what's in question here.
feedback.firm-lied: Possible in principle, but it's the least likely and least useful explanation to default to — an unmeasured adoption gap is a far more common and far more addressable cause than assuming bad faith.

contentSections.mechanism: Outcome pricing ties payment to a behavior change (staff actually working differently) that the consultant can influence but not fully control. A technically sound deliverable can fail to produce the paid-for outcome for reasons — habit, trust, incomplete rollout — that have nothing to do with whether the work itself was good.

contentSections.title: A bounded version that's actually fair

contentSections.scenario: Rather than refuse outcome pricing outright, you propose a bounded version to Denise: a smaller fixed fee, plus a bonus tied to a specific metric.
contentSections.question: Select every element that a bounded, defensible version of this deal actually needs, before it's signed.

items.label: A single, narrowly defined metric (e.g. average minutes per return spent on document re-keying), not “overall savings”
A measured baseline taken before the work starts, from the same source both sides will use to measure after
A fixed measurement window with a start and end date, agreed in advance
An agreement on who runs the measurement and from what data source, so it isn't renegotiated after the fact
Mutual trust that both sides will act in good faith about what counts as savings

explanation.named-metric: Applicable. “Overall savings” invites the attribution dispute from the diagnose-mechanism exercise; a narrow, specific metric doesn't.
explanation.baseline: Applicable. Without a measured before-state from an agreed source, there's no fixed point to measure improvement against — “better than it used to be” becomes a matter of memory and opinion.
explanation.measurement-window: Applicable. An open-ended “we'll see how it goes” window lets either side argue the numbers haven't settled yet, indefinitely.
explanation.who-measures: Applicable. If the measurement source and method aren't agreed upfront, the after-the-fact conversation about whose numbers count becomes its own negotiation.
explanation.verbal-trust: Not applicable as a substitute for the other four. Good faith matters, but the entire reason to specify a metric, baseline, window, and measurer in writing is that memory of what was intended fades and gets renegotiated — trust doesn't survive that the way a written agreement does.

contentSections.synthesis: A defensible outcome-linked bonus needs a named metric, a measured baseline, a fixed window, and an agreed measurer — all in writing, before work starts. Without those four, “we'll split the savings” isn't a pricing structure, it's a disagreement scheduled for six months from now.

contentSections.body: Outcome pricing's appeal is real, and so are its failure points — attribution, measurement, and factors outside your control. A modest fixed fee plus a narrowly defined, pre-measured bonus captures the appeal without the exposure.

title: Scoping around variable capacity, honestly
description: A schedule built on an assumed best week collapses the first time a bad one happens — deliverable-based milestones with real buffer and stated response norms are a more honest scope, and a more reliable one for the client too.

learningObjectives.text: Convert an hours-based, best-case schedule into deliverable-based milestones with real buffer
State response-time norms in a scope document rather than leaving them to be assumed

contentSections.title: The schedule that only works on a good week

contentSections.body: Drafting the timeline for Corrigan's discovery phase, the first instinct is: “I can pull the document sample and write the format inventory in two focused days, so let's say discovery is done by Friday.” That schedule is true exactly once — on a week where nothing goes wrong, nothing else competes for the same two days, and capacity holds steady the whole way through. It's not a lie, but it's a best-case number presented as a plan, and a client who hears “Friday” treats it as a commitment, not an optimistic guess.

Scoping honestly around variable capacity — whether the cause is a chronic condition, a second client, or just a realistically unpredictable week — isn't about admitting less can be delivered. It's about naming the schedule as what it actually is.

Three changes make the difference. **Deliverable-based milestones, not hours-based ones**: “format inventory delivered by [date]” survives a bad day inside the window; “16 hours of my time this week” doesn't, and either gets silently broken or forces working through a day that shouldn't be worked through. **Real buffer, stated as buffer**: if two focused days is the honest estimate, the milestone date is set for five or six calendar days out — not to pad the price, but because a plan with zero slack is a plan that breaks on the first ordinary interruption. **Stated response-time norms**: telling the client upfront — “expect a response within two business days, not same-day” — turns a potential silent gap into an agreed norm nobody has to wonder about.

The honest version of this scope isn't less professional than the optimistic one. It's the version that actually holds.

contentSections.problem: Turn “discovery done by Friday, two focused days of work” into a deliverable-based, buffered milestone for Corrigan's scope document.

steps.label: Name the deliverable, not the hours
steps.work: “A written document-format inventory covering Corrigan's last filing season, categorized by type and edge case” — not “two days of my time.”
steps.why: A deliverable is checkable by the client and survives however many actual hours, across however many actual days, it took to produce — an hours commitment doesn't survive a bad day without either being broken or being pushed through anyway.

steps.label: Set the date with real buffer, and say so
steps.work: Instead of Friday (this week), the milestone is set for the following Wednesday — stated in the scope document as: “estimated effort: two focused days; scheduled window: five business days, to allow for a lower-capacity day without slipping the date.”
steps.why: Naming the buffer explicitly, rather than hiding it inside a padded-but-unexplained date, lets the client see the actual estimate and the actual protection separately — which builds more trust than either an unrealistic tight date or an unexplained loose one.

steps.label: State the response-time norm in writing
steps.work: Add to the scope document: “During this phase, expect replies to questions within two business days. If something is genuinely time-sensitive, flag it as urgent and expect same-day acknowledgment, if not full resolution.”
steps.why: Without a stated norm, silence for a day and a half reads as a red flag to an anxious client. With a stated norm, the identical silence is simply Tuesday.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. The build phase for the extraction pipeline itself is estimated at “about six focused days of work.” Turn this into a deliverable-based, buffered milestone.

blanks.prompt: What's the deliverable, stated so the client can check it themselves?
blanks.answer: A working extraction pipeline that processes the document types named in the format inventory, tested against a held-out sample of Corrigan's own documents, with results logged
accept: a tested, working pipeline covering the inventoried document types, with logged results
blanks.why: Checkable means the client can look at the thing and agree it exists — an hours number gives them nothing to check against.

blanks.prompt: What's a reasonable buffered window and how would it be stated?
blanks.answer: Roughly two calendar weeks for six focused days of estimated work, stated explicitly as: 'estimated effort: six focused days; scheduled window: two weeks, to allow for lower-capacity days without slipping the delivery date'
accept: about double the estimated effort in calendar time, stated explicitly as buffer, not hidden
blanks.why: The buffer ratio isn't a fixed formula, but doubling a multi-day estimate is a defensible starting point, and stating it as buffer — not silently padding the number — is what makes it trustworthy rather than evasive.

blanks.prompt: What response-time norm belongs alongside this milestone?
blanks.answer: The same stated norm as before — replies within two business days, same-day acknowledgment for anything explicitly flagged urgent — restated so it applies across the whole build phase, not just discovery
accept: restate the two-business-day norm for this phase too
blanks.why: A norm stated once for discovery and silently dropped for the build phase leaves a gap exactly where a longer, harder phase makes it more likely to matter.

faded.procedure: For every phase: state the deliverable the client can check, set a calendar window with real buffer stated as buffer rather than hidden inside the date, and restate the response-time norm so it isn't assumed to apply only to the first phase that mentioned it.

contentSections.title: Why this is the more reliable scope, not the less ambitious one

contentSections.question: Put these in the order that turns an optimistic, hours-based estimate into an honest, buffered, deliverable-based milestone.
steps: Estimate the focused effort required, in days, based on the actual work
State the deliverable in a form the client can check for themselves
Set a calendar window meaningfully longer than the effort estimate, and label the gap as buffer explicitly
State the response-time norm that applies during this window
contentSections.explanation: The effort estimate has to come first because everything else is built from it. Stating the deliverable next, before the date, keeps the milestone anchored to something checkable rather than to a number of hours nobody outside the engagement can verify. The buffered window comes after both, because it's calculated from the effort estimate, and it has to be labeled as buffer — an unexplained loose date reads as padding, a labeled one reads as planning. The response-time norm comes last because it applies to the whole window just set, and stating it after the window exists (rather than as a vague general policy) ties it to this specific milestone.

contentSections.body: A schedule that only works on a good week isn't optimistic, it's inaccurate. Deliverable-based milestones with stated buffer and stated response norms are the version of the scope that actually holds — for the consultant and for the client.

title: What's explicitly not included
description: A scope without a written exclusions list doesn't have fewer assumptions baked in — it just has all of them unstated, ready to surface later as “well, obviously that was included.”

learningObjectives.text: Write an exclusions list that names what a scope does not cover, specifically enough to prevent silent scope creep
Recognize when a missing exclusions section is the actual cause of a later scope dispute

contentSections.title: The sentence that isn't in the document

contentSections.body: The Corrigan scope document names the deliverable clearly: a document-intake extraction pipeline for W-2s, 1099s, and standard receipts, tested against Corrigan's own documents, handed over with a runbook. Six weeks after launch, Priya emails: “when are you adding support for the scanned mileage logs the trucking clients send? And we assumed you'd keep tuning it as we hit new formats through the rest of the season — that's still coming, right?” Nothing in the signed document promised either of those things. Nothing in it ruled them out, either.

A scope document that only lists what's included doesn't have fewer unstated assumptions than one with an exclusions section — it has exactly as many, just invisible until someone acts on one. “Obviously that's included” is not a sign the client is being unreasonable; it's what happens by default when a boundary was never drawn out loud.

A real exclusions list names, specifically, what the current scope does not cover: **ongoing model retraining** after handover (a one-time tuning pass is included; adapting to new formats discovered after launch is a separate, priced engagement); **integration with a not-yet-selected practice-management system** (the pipeline outputs to a defined format; wiring it into whatever system Corrigan eventually picks is out of scope until that decision is made); **non-English documents** (the extraction models and validation logic are built and tested against English-language documents only); **production monitoring beyond 30 days post-launch** (after the 30-day window, monitoring becomes Corrigan's responsibility or a separate support arrangement); **training beyond one 90-minute session** (additional sessions, or training for staff hired after the session, are billed separately).

Each exclusion is written as a specific boundary, not a vague disclaimer — specific enough that when a request like Priya's arrives, the answer is already written down, not improvised under pressure.

contentSections.intro: Assemble the exclusions section for Corrigan's document-intake scope, one boundary at a time.

fields.prompt: How should the scope state its position on document formats discovered after launch (like the mileage logs)?

options.label: “We'll do our best to keep the pipeline current”
“The pipeline is built and tested against the document types in the discovery-phase inventory; a document type discovered after launch is a separately scoped and priced addition”
Leave it unstated, since the inventory already lists the covered types

feedback.vague-best-effort: “Best effort” sounds reassuring and settles nothing — it doesn't say whether a new format gets fixed for free, in a week, or ever, which is exactly the ambiguity that produced Priya's email.
feedback.specific-boundary: Correct. This states plainly what's covered (the inventoried types), what a new format means (a separate scoped addition), and doesn't promise open-ended free maintenance.
feedback.silent: The inventory lists what's covered, but silence on what happens when something outside it shows up is precisely the gap Priya's email fell into — the exclusions section exists to close gaps the inclusions list doesn't address.

fields.prompt: Corrigan hasn't yet chosen a practice-management system to eventually receive the pipeline's output. How should that be scoped?

options.label: Include integration with whichever system Corrigan eventually chooses, since it's part of “making this useful”
State that the pipeline delivers output in a defined, documented format; integration into a specific downstream system is a separate, future-scoped piece of work once that system is chosen

feedback.assume-integration: This commits to an unknown — a system that doesn't exist yet, with unknown integration requirements — inside a fixed scope, which is the exact mistake the pricing lesson warned against.
feedback.defined-output-only: Correct. The pipeline's responsibility ends at producing well-defined, documented output; connecting it to a specific future system is honestly a different, not-yet-scopeable piece of work.

fields.prompt: How long should post-launch monitoring be included before it becomes Corrigan's responsibility or a separate arrangement?

options.label: Indefinitely, as part of good service
30 days post-launch, stated explicitly, after which monitoring is Corrigan's responsibility or a separately arranged support engagement

feedback.indefinite: “Good service” isn't a scope boundary — it's the sentiment that makes indefinite free monitoring feel obligatory once it's been happening for months, exactly the trap this lesson is naming.
feedback.thirty-days-stated: Correct. A stated window with a named handoff (to Corrigan, or to a separate paid arrangement) gives both sides a clear point where responsibility changes hands, agreed in advance rather than discovered in an awkward conversation later.

contentSections.synthesis: Each boundary in a real exclusions list does the same job: it takes something that would otherwise be assumed by default — continued free maintenance, absorbed future integration, indefinite monitoring — and states, specifically, where the current scope actually stops. That's what lets “well, obviously” get answered with “actually, here's what we agreed” instead of an argument.

contentSections.title: What a missing exclusions section actually costs

contentSections.code:
Corrigan scope document (excerpt) — no exclusions section:

“Deliverable: a document-intake extraction pipeline for Corrigan's client tax documents, tested and handed over with a runbook. Includes staff training and post-launch support.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw here — not a missing feature, but a structural gap in the document itself?

options.label: “Client tax documents” and “post-launch support” are both undefined-boundary phrases with no stated limits, so every later disagreement about what counts becomes a negotiation instead of a lookup
The deliverable itself is badly written and needs more technical detail
Training and support shouldn't be included in the scope at all

feedback.undefined-boundaries: Correct. “Client tax documents” doesn't say which formats or languages; “post-launch support” doesn't say how long or at what level. Both phrases sound complete and specific while leaving the actual boundary undrawn — which is what an exclusions section exists to fix.
feedback.needs-more-tech-detail: The technical description is fine for what it is — the gap isn't about technical specificity, it's about the document never stating what falls outside these phrases.
feedback.shouldnt-include-training: Training and support are reasonable things to include — the problem isn't that they're there, it's that neither has a stated boundary (how much training, how long the support window), so both quietly expand to whatever the client assumes.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A scope document can name real deliverables accurately and still leave every boundary undrawn, because inclusion language (“includes X”) doesn't automatically imply a limit. The fix isn't rewriting the inclusions — it's adding a parallel exclusions section that states, in the same document, what “client tax documents” and “post-launch support” specifically do not cover.

contentSections.body: An exclusions section isn't defensive paperwork — it's the other half of the scope. What isn't written down as excluded gets assumed as included, and that assumption always surfaces at the least convenient moment.

title: Practice — Scope and Bound Seven Vague Enquiries
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given a vague enquiry or a scoping decision, apply this module's disambiguation, pricing, and exclusions skills.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's enquiry-disambiguation and pricing-structure skills to new briefs
Identify missing exclusions and unbounded pricing in a draft scope

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing is timed, and the set doesn't expire — do all seven now or split them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the lab — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Write a Full Scope and Price for a Real Brief
description: Take a vague enquiry from Marchetti & Sons Property Management, disambiguate it, choose and structure a pricing model, write the exclusions, and set buffered, deliverable-based payment points.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a complete scope document — deliverables, exclusions, assumptions, price, and payment points — from a vague enquiry
Justify pricing and milestone choices against the risks named in this module

contentSections.body: Marchetti & Sons Property Management, a company managing about 900 rental units across a dozen apartment buildings, emails: “We want AI to help handle tenant maintenance requests — it's a mess and something's got to give.” That's the whole enquiry. This lab is running this module's full process against it, from disambiguation through a priced, bounded scope document.

contentSections.title: A full scope and price for Marchetti & Sons
contentSections.brief: Starting from the one-sentence enquiry above, produce a real scope document the way it would actually be sent to a client: which distinct project this is (after disambiguation), a pricing structure with a stated reason, an exclusions and assumptions list, and buffered, deliverable-based payment points.
contentSections.deliverable: A scope document: the disambiguated project statement, at least three follow-up questions you'd actually ask (and what each is trying to find out), a pricing structure with justification, an exclusions list of at least four items, and a payment-point schedule with stated buffer.

stages.title: Disambiguate the enquiry
stages.instructions: “Help handle tenant maintenance requests” could mean intake triage (routing requests to the right vendor/category), status communication with tenants, scheduling coordination with contractors, a knowledge base of which issues need which licensed trade, or fraud/urgency screening (a claimed emergency versus a routine request). Name at least three distinct candidate projects this sentence could mean, then write three follow-up questions that would actually tell them apart — not questions about volume or tooling.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least three named candidate projects and three disambiguating follow-up questions, each tied to a specific candidate.

stages.title: Choose and structure the pricing model
stages.instructions: Assume Marchetti's answers point at intake triage as the real bottleneck, but the range of maintenance-request types (and how cleanly they map to a fixed category list) is unknown. Choose fixed price, T&M, or a hybrid with a priced discovery phase, and justify the choice by naming specifically where each alternative would have bitten.
stages.checkpoint: You have a chosen pricing structure with a written justification naming at least one risk of the structure you didn't choose.

stages.title: Write exclusions and assumptions
stages.instructions: Write at least four exclusions, each a specific boundary (not a vague disclaimer) — consider new request categories discovered after launch, integration with whatever property-management software Marchetti eventually confirms, multi-language tenant requests, and the length of post-launch monitoring. Also list the assumptions the scope depends on (e.g. a minimum volume or format of sample requests Marchetti will provide during discovery).
stages.checkpoint: You have at least four specific exclusions and at least two named assumptions the scope depends on.

stages.title: Set buffered, deliverable-based payment points
stages.instructions: Write at least two payment milestones, each tied to a checkable deliverable (not an hours count), with a calendar window that includes stated buffer beyond the raw effort estimate, and a stated response-time norm for the phase.
stages.checkpoint: Each payment point names a deliverable, a buffered date with the buffer stated explicitly, and a response-time norm.

rubric.criterion: The enquiry is genuinely disambiguated, not just restated
rubric.meets: At least three distinct candidate projects are named, each different enough to imply a different scope.

rubric.criterion: Follow-up questions actually disambiguate
rubric.meets: Each question is tied to telling specific candidates apart, not to volume or tooling preferences.

rubric.criterion: The pricing structure is justified against a named risk
rubric.meets: The write-up states what would have gone wrong with at least one alternative structure, not just which one was picked.

rubric.criterion: Exclusions are specific boundaries, not disclaimers
rubric.meets: Each of the four-plus exclusions names a concrete thing that is out of scope and what happens if it comes up.

rubric.criterion: Payment points are deliverable-based with stated buffer
rubric.meets: Each milestone names a checkable artefact and a calendar window visibly longer than the raw effort estimate, with the gap explained as buffer.

rubric.criterion: A response-time norm is stated, not assumed
rubric.meets: At least one explicit sentence tells the client what response time to expect during the engagement.

contentSections.body: A scope built this way survives contact with an actual messy client, because most of what would otherwise be assumed — which project, what price protects whom, what's excluded, what the timeline really means — has already been written down.

title: Checkpoint — Scoping and Pricing
description: Ten questions, all from this module — the first module of the phase, so there's nothing earlier in it to pull from yet. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's disambiguation, pricing-structure, and exclusions distinctions without looking them up

questions.from: This module — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: Priya's enquiry names “help with tax season.” What's the first job, before proposing anything?

options.label: Enumerate the distinct plausible projects the sentence could mean, then ask questions that tell them apart
Propose the most common AI use case for accounting firms
Ask for a budget number so pricing can start

questions.explanation: A vague enquiry names a feeling, not a task — the first job is separating the plausible distinct projects it could mean and asking questions specific enough to tell them apart.

questions.from: This module — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: “Which of these problems costs the firm the most in overtime hours right now” is a useful disambiguating question. Why, specifically?

options.label: It turns a vague feeling into a specific, comparable fact that points at one candidate project over another
It's useful mainly because it helps set the price
It isn't actually more useful than asking about total return volume

questions.explanation: Disambiguating questions ask for a specific sequence, moment, or cost — total volume is a real number but doesn't tell candidate projects apart the way a cost-comparison question does.

questions.from: This module — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: Fixed price, T&M, and a hybrid discovery-then-fixed-build structure each move risk somewhere. Where does fixed price bite?

options.label: The consultant, if the actual work turns out messier than assumed
The client, since they're locked into paying regardless of quality
Nobody — fixed price removes risk entirely

questions.explanation: Fixed price bites the consultant specifically when the real work is bigger or messier than the quote assumed — the difference gets absorbed or renegotiated awkwardly.

questions.from: This module — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: What's the actual purpose of a priced discovery phase in a hybrid pricing structure?

options.label: To convert an unmeasured range into a written inventory, on a small bounded budget, before a fixed price is attached to the build
To give the consultant more billable hours before the real work starts
To delay the client from asking about price

questions.explanation: A discovery phase's job is turning an unknown range into a counted, written inventory on a small fixed budget, so the build's fixed price is grounded in something real instead of a guess.

questions.from: This module — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: Denise proposes paying a percentage of staff-hours saved. What's the attribution problem with this, specifically?

options.label: Other changes (new hires, tax-law complexity, adoption habits) can move the hours number for reasons that have nothing to do with the consultant's work
Staff hours can't be measured at all
There's no attribution problem — outcome pricing is always fair

questions.explanation: Attribution fails when something other than the delivered work moves the measured outcome — new hires, changed complexity, or an adoption gap can all suppress or inflate the number independent of work quality.

questions.from: This module — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: A bounded, defensible outcome-linked bonus needs which four elements, agreed before work starts?

options.label: A named narrow metric, a measured baseline, a fixed measurement window, and an agreed measurer/data source
A handshake agreement and mutual good faith
An open-ended “we'll see how it goes” review period

questions.explanation: Without a named metric, baseline, window, and agreed measurer, an outcome-linked bonus becomes a disagreement scheduled for months in the future rather than a pricing structure.

questions.from: This module — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: Why is “two focused days, so it'll be done Friday” a risky way to schedule a milestone?

options.label: It states a best-case number as a plan with no buffer for an ordinary bad day or interruption
Two days is always too optimistic an estimate for any task
Fridays are a bad day of the week to schedule deliveries

questions.explanation: The problem isn't the estimate itself, it's presenting a best-case number as a commitment with zero slack — buffer stated explicitly is what makes the milestone survive a normal bad day.

questions.from: This module — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: What makes a milestone “deliverable-based” rather than “hours-based,” and why does that matter?

options.label: It names a checkable artefact the client can verify, which survives however many actual hours or days it took — unlike an hours commitment, which breaks on a bad day
It's the same thing, just phrased differently
It matters only for billing purposes, not for reliability

questions.explanation: A deliverable is something the client can check for themselves regardless of how the underlying hours actually played out — an hours commitment is fragile to exactly the variability this lesson is about.

questions.from: This module — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: Priya assumes ongoing free format support was included, because the scope document never said otherwise. What's the actual cause of that assumption?

options.label: The scope document had no exclusions section, so every unstated boundary defaulted to “included” in the client's mind
Priya is being unreasonable
The inclusions list should have been longer

questions.explanation: A scope without a written exclusions section doesn't have fewer boundaries — it has all of them unstated, which defaults to “obviously included” in the client's reading.

questions.from: This module — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: What makes an exclusion useful, versus a vague disclaimer that doesn't actually prevent a later dispute?

options.label: It names a specific boundary and states what happens if that situation comes up (e.g. a separately priced addition), not just a general reassurance
Length — a longer exclusions section is always more useful
Legal language — exclusions only work if phrased formally

questions.explanation: “We'll do our best” settles nothing; a specific boundary with a stated consequence (a separately scoped addition, a defined handoff point) is what actually prevents the later “well, obviously” argument.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: The number in the sponsor's head that nobody said out loud
description: A sponsor's offhand remark in a kickoff call can quietly become the standard the whole engagement gets judged against — the fix is asking directly what success looks like in a specific, measurable term before the call ends.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize an offhand kickoff remark as an unscoped success metric forming in real time
Ask a direct question that surfaces the sponsor's actual, specific success criterion before the kickoff ends

contentSections.body: The scope is signed: a document-intake extraction pipeline for Corrigan Tax & Advisory, tested against real documents, cutting the time staff spend re-keying client paperwork. In the kickoff call, Denise Marsh says, almost as an aside while moving to the next agenda item: “so by April we basically won't need Walt double-checking every single return anymore, right?” Nobody scoped eliminating Walt's review. The scope promised faster intake, not fewer review steps. If this sentence goes unanswered, it doesn't disappear — it becomes the thing Denise judges April against.

This is the same mechanism a stray, unscoped sentence always follows in a client relationship: whatever specific, measurable claim goes unchallenged in the room becomes the implicit definition of success later, whether or not it was ever actually promised. It's easy to let it pass, because correcting it mid-agenda feels like nitpicking a throwaway comment on a call that's going well.

The fix isn't to let it pass and hope it fades, and it isn't to bluntly announce “that's not in scope” either — both read as either evasive or combative. The fix is a direct question: “when you say ‘won't need Walt double-checking,' what would you actually want to see by April — fewer minutes per return, or the review step itself going away?” That question does two things at once: it makes the vague remark concrete, and it puts the actual answer on record while there's still time to agree or correct it, instead of discovering the gap in April.

contentSections.scenario: Denise's remark passes without anyone responding to it directly — the call moves on to timeline questions. Three weeks later, review time per return has genuinely dropped by 40%, but Walt is still reviewing every return, because that was never actually removed from the design.
contentSections.question: Why does this read as a failed engagement to Denise, even though the measured outcome (40% less review time) is a real, significant result?

options.label: The unaddressed kickoff remark quietly became Denise's actual success metric, and the engagement is being judged against that metric instead of the one that was scoped
40% simply isn't a large enough improvement to count as a success by any standard
Walt is at fault for continuing to review returns out of habit

feedback.unscoped-metric-hardened: Correct. Nothing about staying silent on Denise's remark made it go away — it sat there as her actual expectation, unconnected to what was scoped, and now the real, measured 40% improvement is being judged against a standard nobody agreed to.
feedback.40-percent-not-enough: 40% is a substantial result by almost any standard for a first release — the problem isn't the size of the number, it's that it's the wrong number for what Denise is actually checking against.
feedback.walt-fault: Walt reviewing every return isn't a failure of anyone's — it's simply what the actual scope specified. The mismatch is between the scope and Denise's unaddressed expectation, not a performance problem with Walt.

contentSections.mechanism: An unaddressed, specific-sounding remark in a kickoff doesn't get forgotten just because nobody responded to it — it becomes the standard the engagement is judged against later, independent of whether it was ever actually scoped or agreed to.

contentSections.scenario: You want to ask Denise the direct clarifying question without it sounding like you're second-guessing her judgment in front of the room.
contentSections.question: Select every fact that's genuinely knowable and safe to state back to Denise at this point in the kickoff, before any pilot has run.

items.label: What the signed scope actually promises: faster document intake, not review elimination
That Denise just described a specific outcome — review going away — that wasn't part of that scope
Whether eliminating Walt's review step is actually feasible by April
Exactly how much review time per return will drop once the pipeline is live

explanation.scoped-deliverable: Knowable — it's what's already written down and signed. Stating it back is grounding the conversation in fact, not opinion.
explanation.denise-said-it: Knowable — repeating back what was just said, neutrally, is how you make an offhand remark explicit without accusing anyone of anything.
explanation.review-elimination-feasible: Not knowable yet — nobody has tested how the pipeline performs on Corrigan's actual hardest documents, so no one can honestly say whether review could ever safely be removed.
explanation.review-time-drop-amount: Not knowable yet — that's exactly what the pilot exists to measure, and stating a number now would be the identical mistake this lesson opened with, just with different content.

contentSections.synthesis: The safe things to say back are what's already agreed and what was just said — both are facts about the room, not predictions about the system. Predictions about pipeline performance belong after a real pilot, not inside a kickoff clarification.

contentSections.body: An unaddressed, specific-sounding remark in a kickoff becomes the standard the engagement gets judged against later — ask what success would actually look like, in a measurable term, while the room can still agree or correct it.

title: Saying what won't happen, before the kickoff
description: Naming what the deliverable won't do yet, stated proactively in the kickoff agenda, prevents the same gaps a reactive correction has to clean up later — and it's cheap to do while nobody has assumed anything yet.

learningObjectives.text: Convert a scope document's inclusions into explicit, paired statements of what won't happen by the deadline
Distinguish proactive negative-scoping from reactive correction and identify when each is being used

contentSections.title: Correcting a gap versus naming it first

contentSections.body: The previous lesson's fix — asking Denise a direct clarifying question — worked, but it was reactive: it happened because she said something specific enough to catch. Not every unscoped assumption announces itself that clearly. A better kickoff doesn't wait to react to what gets said; it proactively states what the deliverable won't do yet, before anyone in the room has had the chance to assume otherwise.

Proactive negative-scoping means taking the scope document's list of inclusions and pairing each one with an explicit, spoken statement of its boundary — in the kickoff itself, on the agenda, not buried in a document nobody re-reads. For Corrigan's pipeline: “this will cut the time it takes to get a document's fields into the tax software — it will not, this season, remove the review step itself.” “This will handle the document types in our discovery inventory — a format we haven't seen yet gets flagged for manual entry, not guessed at.” “This will be live for the extraction step by [date] — it will not include integration with a new practice-management system, since Corrigan hasn't chosen one yet.”

The difference between this and the previous lesson's reactive correction is timing and posture. Reactive correction happens after someone says something that reveals a gap, and it can feel like walking back an assumption they already made. Proactive negative-scoping happens before anyone has assumed anything, stated in the same breath as what the deliverable *will* do — which reads as thoroughness, not as hedging.

contentSections.problem: Convert the Corrigan scope's core inclusion — “extraction pipeline for W-2s, 1099s, and standard receipts” — into a proactive negative-scoping statement for the kickoff agenda.

steps.label: State the inclusion in plain terms
steps.work: “The pipeline will read incoming W-2s, 1099s, and standard receipts and pull the key fields — vendor, amount, date — straight into the tax software.”
steps.why: Starting with what it does, stated plainly, sets a positive frame before the boundary is named — the sentence isn't primarily about limitation.

steps.label: Name the paired boundary from the exclusions list
steps.work: “It won't yet handle formats outside that list — like the scanned mileage logs from trucking clients — those get flagged for manual entry rather than guessed at, and adding that format is a separate, scoped addition.”
steps.why: Pairing the boundary directly with the inclusion, in the same breath, is what makes it land as a natural continuation of the description rather than a separate, defensive caveat.

steps.label: Say it out loud in the kickoff, not just in the document
steps.work: This sentence gets spoken during the kickoff's scope-review agenda item, with a pause for questions — not left for someone to find later in a document they may not re-read before April.
steps.why: A boundary that only exists in a signed document nobody re-reads under deadline pressure isn't functionally different from a boundary that was never stated — saying it out loud, in the room, at the moment attention is highest, is what actually prevents the later surprise.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. The scope also includes “staff training — one 90-minute session.” Convert this into a proactive negative-scoping statement.

blanks.prompt: State the inclusion in plain terms.
blanks.answer: We'll run one 90-minute training session covering how to use the pipeline and what to do when a document gets flagged for manual entry
accept: one 90-minute session on using the pipeline and handling flagged documents
blanks.why: The plain description names exactly what happens in that session, which is what makes the paired boundary land as a natural next sentence rather than a surprising limitation.

blanks.prompt: Name the paired boundary.
blanks.answer: That one session covers the staff in the room that day — training for anyone hired afterward, or a second session, is billed separately, not included automatically
accept: additional sessions or staff hired later aren't automatically covered, and would be a separate cost
blanks.why: Without naming this boundary, a new hire in June with no training becomes a support request that reads as the consultant having failed to deliver something that was never actually promised.

blanks.prompt: Where and how should this actually get said?
blanks.answer: Spoken in the kickoff during the scope-review agenda item, alongside the other paired inclusion/boundary statements, with a moment for Denise or Priya to ask questions
accept: said out loud in the kickoff's scope review, not left only in the written document
blanks.why: Same reasoning as the first case — a spoken boundary at the moment of highest attention is what actually prevents the gap from surfacing as a surprise months later.

faded.procedure: For each major inclusion in the scope: state what it does in plain terms, pair it in the same breath with its actual boundary from the exclusions list, and say both out loud in the kickoff itself — not only in a document that won't get re-read under deadline pressure.

contentSections.question: Put these in the order that builds a proactive negative-scoping agenda item for a kickoff, from the signed scope document.
steps: Pull each major inclusion from the signed scope document
For each one, find its matching boundary in the exclusions list
Write a paired sentence stating what it does and what it won't do yet, in plain language
Read each paired sentence out loud during the kickoff's scope-review agenda item, pausing for questions
contentSections.explanation: You can't pair a boundary to an inclusion you haven't pulled out first, and matching the two only works because the exclusions list already exists from the scoping module's work. Writing the sentence in plain language matters before reading it aloud, because kickoff calls are the wrong place to be improvising precise phrasing on the fly.
