Reading it aloud with a pause is the step that actually does the work — a written sentence nobody hears has the same effect as no sentence at all.

contentSections.body: Reacting to a stray remark works, but it's a repair. Naming what won't happen yet, in the same breath as what will, before anyone has assumed otherwise, is cheaper and prevents the gap instead of cleaning it up.

title: Pilots that prove something rather than impress someone
description: A pilot built to answer a real go/no-go question and a pilot built to look good in a room are structurally different — one uses the client's own hardest documents, the other quietly avoids them.

learningObjectives.text: Design a pilot that answers a specific, real question using a representative sample including hard cases
Recognize when a proposed pilot design is optimized to impress rather than to inform a decision

contentSections.title: Two different jobs a pilot can do

contentSections.body: Priya suggests running the pilot on “a nice clean batch, so the partners get a good first impression before we get into the messy stuff.” It's a reasonable-sounding instinct — nobody wants the first thing partners see to be a failure. It's also a pilot that answers a different question than the one that actually matters: not “does this work well enough to build on,” but “does this look good enough to keep going.”

A pilot designed to prove something starts from a real, named question — for Corrigan, something like: “on a representative week of actual incoming documents, including the hardest ones, how many fields come out correct without a human fixing them, and which specific document types still need work?” That question requires an honest, representative sample, hard cases included, because a clean sample can't answer it — it can only produce a number that looks good regardless of what the real range would show.

A pilot designed to impress starts from a different, unspoken question: “what sample will make this look successful.” It quietly selects for easy cases, avoids the scanned mileage logs and handwritten notes, and produces a demo that's true and misleading at the same time — true, because the numbers are real; misleading, because they don't represent what production will actually look like. The two pilots can use identical language (“we ran a pilot, here are the results”) while measuring completely different things.

contentSections.code:
Proposed pilot design (Priya's version):

“Pull 15 recent documents that came in clean and complete — no handwritten notes, no odd formats — run extraction, and present the accuracy number at next week's partner meeting.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this design, given that the goal is to inform a real build decision?

options.label: The sample deliberately excludes the hardest cases, so the resulting accuracy number can't answer the real question — how the pipeline handles the full range of documents Corrigan actually receives
15 documents is too small a sample size to be statistically meaningful
Presenting results at a partner meeting is the wrong audience for pilot results

feedback.excludes-hard-cases: Correct. The problem isn't the count, it's the selection — a sample of only clean, complete documents structurally can't produce a number that says anything about how the pipeline handles Corrigan's actual, messier document mix.
feedback.sample-too-small: Sample size is a secondary concern here — even a much larger sample built the same way (clean documents only) would still produce a misleadingly high number, because the selection, not the count, is what's broken.
feedback.wrong-audience: The partner meeting is a reasonable place to present real results — the issue isn't who's in the room, it's that the results being prepared for them don't represent the real situation.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A pilot's sample selection is the whole ballgame — the same accuracy-calculation method run on a curated sample versus a representative one produces two different numbers that both look like “the pilot's result,” and only one of them tells you anything about production. Selecting for clean documents doesn't make the pilot dishonest exactly, but it does make it answer the wrong question convincingly.

contentSections.scenario: You're pushing back on Priya's clean-sample proposal and designing the real pilot instead.
contentSections.question: Select every element the real pilot needs to actually answer the go/no-go question.

items.label: A full, unfiltered batch of documents from one real recent week — whatever actually came in, hard cases included
Results broken down by document type, not blended into one overall number
A stated question the pilot is meant to answer, agreed with Denise before it runs, not decided after seeing the results
A results summary that highlights the successful extractions and mentions failures only if asked

explanation.unfiltered-week: Applicable. An unfiltered real batch is what makes the results representative of what production will actually look like, hard cases included.
explanation.per-type-breakdown: Applicable. A single blended number hides exactly the kind of information Corrigan needs — which specific document types (like the mileage logs) still need work — the same problem the accuracy-blending lesson elsewhere in this track warns about.
explanation.named-question: Applicable. Agreeing on the question in advance is what stops the pilot's framing from being quietly chosen after the fact to match whatever result came out.
explanation.only-successes: Not applicable — this is the impress-rather-than-prove pattern from the spot-flaw exercise, just applied to how results are presented instead of how the sample was selected.

contentSections.synthesis: A pilot that proves something uses an unfiltered, representative sample, breaks results down by type instead of blending them, agrees its question in advance, and reports the failures as plainly as the successes. Each of these is what a pilot built to impress quietly skips.

contentSections.body: A pilot's job is to answer a real question honestly, not to produce a good-looking number. Use a representative sample, hard cases included, and agree the question before you see the results.

title: Demos and the gap between demo and production
description: A clean, curated demo is true and can still set an expectation that production can't hold — the gap has to be named at demo time, not discovered afterward.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a demo's framing risks becoming the client's implicit definition of the finished product
State the gap between demo and production explicitly, at demo time, without undercutting the demo's real result

contentSections.title: A true demo that still misleads

contentSections.body: The honest pilot from the last lesson worked well: on a representative week's documents, the pipeline correctly extracted fields from the standard, clean W-2s and 1099s nearly every time — genuinely good, real results. For the partner-meeting demo, it makes sense to show that part live; nobody wants to spend a demo slot on the known hard cases. Walt watches the demo, turns to Denise, and says: “so it's basically done, right?”

Nothing shown in the demo was false. The gap is between what a demo can practically show (a handful of representative-of-the-easy-part examples, in a controlled setting, in a few minutes) and what production actually is (the full range of documents, over months, unattended). A demo that only shows what works well, without saying so, doesn't lie — it lets the audience's imagination fill in the rest, and the rest usually gets filled in as “this, but for everything.”

The fix isn't avoiding demos, or diluting a good result by leading with the hard cases. It's naming the gap explicitly, right at the moment the demo lands well: “what you just saw is real, on real documents — and it's the easier half of the mix. The harder formats, like the scanned mileage logs, are what the next phase of work focuses on; today they'd get flagged for manual entry instead of guessed at.” Said at the moment of the demo's strongest impression, this doesn't undercut the result — it's what keeps the result from becoming a promise nobody made.

contentSections.title: Walt asks the question live, in the room
contentSections.opening: The demo just landed well. Walt, watching, asks out loud: “so it's basically done, right?” Denise is nodding along, waiting for the answer.

asked.situation: Every eye in the room is on you.
asked.question: What's the right response?

choices.label: “Yes, exactly — this is what you'll be using”
choices.consequence: This confirms exactly the gap this lesson is about — the easy-case demo just became, in Walt's and Denise's understanding, the description of the finished product.

choices.label: “The part you just saw is real and it's working well — it's the more standard documents. The harder formats, like the mileage logs, are the next phase; today those get flagged for manual entry”
choices.consequence: This keeps the good result intact while placing it accurately — Walt and Denise now know specifically what's covered and what isn't, without the demo's impact being undercut.

choices.label: “Let's not get into the details now, we can talk after the meeting”
choices.consequence: This avoids answering in the room where the expectation is actually forming, and Walt is left to fill in the gap himself — which tends to default to the most optimistic reading, the same failure mode as saying yes.

walt-followup.situation: Walt, satisfied with the honest answer, asks a natural follow-up: “okay — so when do the mileage logs get handled?”
walt-followup.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Name the actual next step and rough timing — e.g. “that's part of the next scoped phase, which we can plan out once this rollout is stable”
choices.consequence: A concrete next step, even a rough one, turns the honest gap into a plan instead of an open question — which is what makes the honesty land as competence rather than as a limitation.

choices.label: “Soon, we're working on it”
choices.consequence: This replaces one vague promise with another — “soon” with no plan behind it tends to get remembered as a specific-sounding commitment the same way Denise's original offhand remark did.

confirmed-gap.summary: The demo's easy-case result becomes, in the room, the description of the finished system. When the mileage logs and handwritten notes show up in production unhandled, it reads as the system breaking, not as an unbuilt phase arriving on schedule.
confirmed-gap.lesson: A true demo, confirmed without qualification under a direct question, becomes exactly the over-promise this module is built to prevent.

deflected.summary: Deflecting avoids an awkward moment in the room, but the room still forms an impression — usually the optimistic one — and now there's no record of what was actually said, since the real answer never got stated.
deflected.lesson: The moment a client asks the direct question is the cheapest moment to answer it honestly — deflecting doesn't remove the expectation, it just removes the chance to shape it accurately.

vague-promise.summary: The gap was named honestly, but 'soon, we're working on it' quietly recreates the same unscoped-promise problem this module opened with, just for the next phase instead of this one.
vague-promise.lesson: Naming a gap honestly only prevents a future over-promise if what comes next is a genuinely stated plan, not another vague reassurance.

honest-and-planned.summary: Walt and Denise leave the meeting with an accurate picture: what's working now, what isn't yet, and a real next step for it — the demo's genuine result stands, without becoming a promise about the parts that weren't shown.
honest-and-planned.lesson: Naming the demo/production gap at the moment of strongest impression, then following it with a concrete next step, is what turns an honest limitation into evidence of a well-run engagement.

contentSections.body: A demo can be entirely true and still set the wrong expectation, because it can only show a slice and the audience fills in the rest. Name the gap at the moment the demo lands, not after someone assumes the whole thing is done.

title: Written expectations, referred back to without drama
description: An expectation that only exists as a memory of what was said in a call becomes a dispute the moment two people remember it differently — a written recap, referred back to neutrally, prevents the dispute rather than winning it.

learningObjectives.text: Write a kickoff recap that captures agreed expectations in a form both sides can refer back to neutrally

contentSections.title: The recap that prevents a later argument

contentSections.body: Everything so far in this module happened out loud — the direct clarifying question, the proactive boundary statements, the honest demo caveat. All of it lives only in the memory of whoever was in the room, and memory is exactly where “I never said that” and “that's definitely what you told us” both feel completely true to the people saying them. Two months from now, whether Walt's review step was ever meant to change is either a two-minute lookup or a tense phone call, depending on whether any of this got written down.

A kickoff recap — a short email sent within a day of the call, to everyone who was in the room — turns spoken agreements into something both sides can point at later without either one having to rely on being believed. It doesn't need to be a formal contract amendment; it needs to name, specifically, what got discussed: “per today's call — the pipeline will cut document-intake time; it will not remove Walt's review step this season. The pilot will run against a full, unfiltered week of documents, hard cases included, and we'll review the per-type breakdown together before the partner demo.”

The value shows up later, and it shows up as the *absence* of drama rather than as a tool for winning an argument. When Denise's April question arrives, the reply isn't “that's not what I said” — it's “per the March 3 kickoff notes, this phase covers intake time, not the review step — here's the message.” Referring back to a shared, dated record is neutral in a way that reciting a memory of a conversation never quite is, for either side.

contentSections.problem: Write the kickoff recap email for the Corrigan call covered in this module's earlier lessons.

steps.label: Open with the date and who was on the call
steps.work: “Recap of our March 3 kickoff call — Denise, Priya, Walt, and [consultant]. Sharing this so we all have the same record to refer back to as the project moves.”
steps.why: Naming the date and attendees upfront is what makes the recap a specific, referenceable record rather than a vague summary someone could later claim they weren't part of.

steps.label: State each agreed boundary in plain, specific language
steps.work: “The pipeline will cut the time to get document fields into the tax software. It will not remove Walt's review step this season — that's a separate, future conversation once we have real production data.”
steps.why: This is the exact proactive negative-scoping sentence from lesson 2, now given a durable, dated home instead of only existing as something said out loud once.

steps.label: State the pilot's agreed design and question
steps.work: “The pilot will run against a full, unfiltered week of real documents — hard cases included — and we'll look at results broken down by document type together before anything gets shown at the partner meeting.”
steps.why: Recording the pilot's design in writing is what prevents the clean-sample version from quietly becoming 'what we agreed to' by default if nobody's tracking it.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. Add the recap's closing section, covering the demo caveat from lesson 4 and inviting corrections.

blanks.prompt: How should the recap state the demo/production gap, in writing, for the record?
blanks.answer: Any demo we show will be a real result on a real sample, and we'll say plainly what's included in that sample and what isn't yet — the goal is that nobody leaves a demo assuming more was shown than actually was
accept: demos will show real results and explicitly state what they do and don't cover
blanks.why: Writing this down before any demo happens means it's an agreed norm going in, not a caveat improvised defensively after someone's already formed the wrong impression.

blanks.prompt: How should the email invite correction, so the recap itself doesn't become a one-sided record?
blanks.answer: A closing line like: 'If anything here doesn't match what you understood from the call, reply and let's sort it out now, while it's easy to fix'
accept: explicitly invite anyone to correct the recap if their understanding differs
blanks.why: A recap that's silently treated as final, with no invitation to correct it, can itself become a one-sided version of events — inviting correction while it's still cheap to fix is what makes it a shared record instead of a unilateral one.

faded.procedure: A kickoff recap works because it's dated, specific, sent promptly, and open to correction while correcting it is still cheap — not because it's long, formal, or legally binding. The goal is a shared reference point, not a gotcha document.

contentSections.title: Referring back without it sounding like a fight

contentSections.body: An expectation that only lives in memory becomes a dispute the moment two people remember it differently. A dated, specific, promptly sent recap — open to correction — turns a later disagreement into a two-minute lookup instead of a phone call nobody wants to make.

title: Practice — Rewrite Seven Over-Promises Into Commitments You Can Keep
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given an over-promise, a vague pilot plan, or an unrecorded verbal agreement, apply this module's expectation-setting skills.

learningObjectives.text: Rewrite vague or over-promising statements into specific, bounded commitments
Identify unscoped assumptions and pilot-design flaws in new scenarios

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing is timed, and the set doesn't expire — do all seven now or split them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the lab — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Run a Kickoff That Surfaces the Unstated Expectation
description: Run a simulated kickoff for a new client, Solano Behavioral Health Group, finding and resolving the unstated expectations before they harden — and write the recap that makes the resolution durable.

learningObjectives.text: Identify unstated expectations forming in a live kickoff scenario and resolve each one explicitly
Produce a written kickoff record naming every expectation found and how it was resolved

contentSections.body: Solano Behavioral Health Group, a practice of eleven therapists, has scoped and signed a project: an AI tool that drafts a first-pass session note from a therapist's brief spoken summary after each session, for the therapist to review and finalize. The kickoff call is about to happen. This lab runs it.

contentSections.title: Surface and resolve the unstated expectations
contentSections.brief: During the kickoff, the practice's founder, Dr. Renata Ibarra, makes several remarks — some are innocuous scheduling comments, and at least two are unstated success-metric assumptions the size of Denise's “Walt won't need to review” comment from this module. Find them, resolve each one the way this module's lessons taught, and write it up.
contentSections.deliverable: A kickoff record: a transcript-style set of at least 5 remarks from the simulated kickoff (you can write these, grounded in a therapy-practice context), which ones were unstated expectations versus which were genuinely innocuous, how each expectation was resolved in the room, and the written recap email sent afterward.

stages.title: Draft the kickoff's remarks and flag the expectation-forming ones
stages.instructions: Write at least 5 plausible remarks Dr. Ibarra or her office manager might make during a kickoff for this project — mix genuinely innocuous ones (scheduling, room logistics) with at least two that quietly assume something unscoped (e.g. a specific accuracy bar, a claim about not needing to review drafts eventually, a timeline that wasn't actually agreed). Flag which is which and explain why.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least 5 remarks, with at least 2 correctly flagged as unstated-expectation risks and a reason for each.

stages.title: Resolve each flagged expectation in the room
stages.instructions: For each flagged remark, write the direct clarifying question or proactive boundary statement you'd actually say in response, the way this module's lessons modeled — not a vague deflection.
stages.checkpoint: Each flagged remark has a specific, spoken resolution attached to it, not a generic 'we'll clarify later.'

stages.title: Write the kickoff recap email
stages.instructions: Write the full recap email: date and attendees, each resolved expectation stated plainly, the pilot's agreed design (representative sample, hard cases included, per-type breakdown), and a closing line inviting correction.
stages.checkpoint: The recap covers every resolved expectation from stage 2, states the pilot design, and invites correction.

rubric.criterion: At least two genuine unstated-expectation risks are correctly identified
rubric.meets: Each flagged remark is explained in terms of what unscoped assumption it quietly makes, not just labeled 'risky.'

rubric.criterion: Innocuous remarks are correctly distinguished from real risks
rubric.meets: At least one remark is identified as genuinely innocuous, with a reason it doesn't carry an unscoped assumption.

rubric.criterion: Each risk has a specific, spoken resolution
rubric.meets: The resolution is a real sentence you'd say in the room, not a note-to-self to address it eventually.

rubric.criterion: The pilot design follows this module's standard
rubric.meets: The recap's pilot description names an unfiltered, representative sample and a per-type results breakdown, not a curated one.

rubric.criterion: The recap is dated, specific, and invites correction
rubric.meets: The email names the date and attendees, states expectations plainly, and has a closing line inviting anyone to correct it.

contentSections.body: The skill in this module isn't reacting well once — it's running a whole kickoff assuming several unstated expectations are forming somewhere in the room, and finding them before the call ends.

title: Checkpoint — Setting Expectations That Hold
description: Ten questions, all from this module — modules 1 and 2 of the phase are relaxed on the 40/40/20 pull, since there's not yet enough of the phase behind them to pull from meaningfully. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's expectation-setting, pilot-design, and written-record distinctions without looking them up

questions.from: This module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: Denise says “by April we won't need Walt double-checking every return, right?” and the call moves on. What actually happens to that remark if nobody responds to it?

options.label: It becomes Denise's implicit success metric, regardless of whether it was ever actually scoped
It's forgotten by the time April arrives, since it was said casually
It has no real effect, since only the signed scope document legally matters

questions.explanation: An unaddressed, specific-sounding remark doesn't vanish just because it wasn't scoped — it becomes the standard the sponsor judges the engagement against later.

questions.from: This module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: What's the actual fix for a remark like Denise's, in the moment?

options.label: Ask directly what success would specifically look like, putting the real answer on record while there's still time to agree or correct it
Let it pass, since correcting a stray comment feels like nitpicking
Bluntly announce it's out of scope and move on

questions.explanation: A direct clarifying question makes the vague remark concrete and puts the real answer on record early — neither ignoring it nor a blunt dismissal does that.

questions.from: This module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: What's the difference between proactive negative-scoping and reactive correction?

options.label: Proactive scoping states boundaries before anyone assumes otherwise; reactive correction only responds after a gap-revealing remark happens
They're the same technique with different names
Reactive correction is always the better approach since it responds to real signals

questions.explanation: Proactive scoping doesn't wait for a remark that reveals a gap — it states the boundary alongside the inclusion, before anyone has had the chance to assume otherwise.

questions.from: This module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: Why does pairing an inclusion and its boundary in the same breath work better than stating the boundary separately later?

options.label: It reads as thoroughness rather than as a separate, defensive caveat added afterward
It doesn't actually matter when the boundary is stated
Boundaries stated later are always more credible

questions.explanation: A boundary paired with its inclusion in the same sentence lands as a natural continuation of the description; the same boundary stated separately, later, tends to read as hedging or backpedaling.

questions.from: This module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: Priya proposes running the pilot on 15 clean, complete documents. What's the actual flaw?

options.label: The sample deliberately excludes hard cases, so it can't answer the real question about how the pipeline handles Corrigan's actual document mix
15 documents is too small a sample to be statistically valid
A partner meeting is the wrong venue for pilot results

questions.explanation: The flaw is selection, not count — excluding the hardest cases produces a number that can't speak to real production performance, regardless of how many clean documents are in the sample.

questions.from: This module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: What does a pilot need, per this module, to actually answer a real go/no-go question?

options.label: An unfiltered representative sample, results broken down by type, and a question agreed before results are seen
The largest possible sample size, regardless of composition
A presentation that highlights successes and mentions failures only if asked

questions.explanation: Representativeness, per-type breakdown, and a pre-agreed question are what make a pilot's result mean something — sample size alone and success-only reporting don't.

questions.from: This module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: The Corrigan demo shows the pipeline working well on standard W-2s and 1099s. Why can this be entirely true and still mislead?

options.label: A demo can only show a slice in a few minutes, and an audience tends to fill in the rest of the picture as 'this, but for everything'
It can't mislead if every individual claim shown is factually accurate
Demos are inherently dishonest by nature

questions.explanation: The gap isn't in any single claim being false — it's between what a short demo can practically show and what production actually is, and an audience's imagination tends to fill that gap optimistically.

questions.from: This module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: When Walt asks live, “so it's basically done, right?”, what's the response that both preserves the demo's real result and prevents the over-promise?

options.label: Confirming what was shown is real, while naming specifically what wasn't covered and isn't done yet
A flat yes, since the demo genuinely did work well
Deflecting the question until after the meeting

questions.explanation: Confirming the real result while naming the specific gap keeps the demo's impact intact without letting it become a claim about the whole system — a flat yes or a deflection both let the room form the wrong impression.

questions.from: This module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: Why does a written kickoff recap actually prevent a later dispute, rather than just document one after it happens?

options.label: It gives both sides a shared, dated reference to point to, so a disagreement becomes a lookup instead of a contest of two different memories
It legally binds the client to every word spoken in the kickoff
It doesn't actually prevent disputes, only documents them for later

questions.explanation: The value is in having a shared, neutral reference — referring back to a dated record is fundamentally different from each side reciting their own memory of what was said.

questions.from: This module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: What makes a kickoff recap a shared record instead of a one-sided one?

options.label: It's sent promptly and includes an explicit invitation to correct it while correcting it is still cheap
It's written in formal legal language
It's sent only to the sponsor, not the whole kickoff group

questions.explanation: A recap sent to everyone, promptly, with an open invitation to correct it, is what keeps it a genuinely shared reference rather than one person's unilateral version of the call.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Explaining the mechanism in ninety seconds
description: A compressed capability explanation has a fixed shape — what it does, how it actually works, what it doesn't do, why that matters — and skipping any one of the four leaves a decision-maker with an inflated or confused picture.

learningObjectives.text: Construct a ninety-second capability explanation covering function, mechanism, limits, and relevance in order

contentSections.title: Explaining AI to People Who Don't Care How It Works

contentSections.body: Denise Marsh puts her head around the door: “give me ninety seconds on how this actually works — the partners meeting starts now, and Greg's already asking questions.” No time for a deck, no time for jargon, and no time to explain it twice. What comes out in the next ninety seconds either sets the partners up to make a reasonable decision or sends them into the meeting with either an inflated picture or no picture at all.

A compressed explanation that actually works has a fixed shape, in order: **what it does** (one plain sentence — the function, not the technology); **how it actually works, at a mechanism level** (one or two sentences, no jargon, enough that “how” isn't a black box, without a lecture on model architecture); **what it doesn't do** (one sentence — the boundary, stated as plainly as the capability); **why that matters for the decision at hand** (the close — connects the previous three sentences to whatever the room actually needs to decide).

Skipping the mechanism sentence leaves the capability sounding like magic, which either triggers suspicion or invites over-trust. Skipping the limits sentence is how a true, accurate description becomes an over-promise the moment nobody says what it doesn't do. Skipping the close leaves four sentences of information with no reason for a non-technical partner to act on any of it. All four fit in ninety seconds because each one is a single sentence, not a paragraph.

contentSections.intro: Assemble the ninety-second explanation of Corrigan's extraction pipeline, one sentence at a time.

fields.prompt: What does it do — stated as function, not technology?

options.label: “It's a large language model with a document-processing layer”
“It reads an incoming client document and fills in the fields our staff currently type by hand”

feedback.tech-first: This names the technology before saying what it's for — for a room deciding whether to invest in this, the function has to come first; the technology is a supporting detail, not the headline.
feedback.function-first: Correct. This states plainly what changes for the people in the room, without requiring anyone to already know what a 'document-processing layer' is.

fields.prompt: How does it actually work, at a mechanism level a non-technical partner can hold onto?

options.label: “It uses transformer-based attention mechanisms trained on labeled document datasets”
“It's been shown examples of our real documents with the correct fields marked, and it learned to spot the same patterns in a new one”

feedback.too-technical: This is accurate and useless to the room — it answers 'how does it work' with vocabulary that requires its own explanation, which defeats the purpose of a mechanism sentence in a compressed briefing.
feedback.right-level: Correct. This gives a real mechanism — pattern-matching from labeled examples — in language that doesn't require any technical background, which is exactly the bar a mechanism sentence needs to clear.

fields.prompt: What does it not do — the boundary sentence?

options.label: Skip this — the mechanism sentence already implies its own limits
“On a document format it hasn't seen a clear example of, it flags the document for a person instead of guessing”

feedback.omit-limits: A mechanism sentence doesn't automatically communicate a limit — most listeners will hear 'it learns patterns' as reassuring, not as a boundary, unless the boundary is stated separately and explicitly.
feedback.state-limits: Correct. This states the actual failure mode in plain terms — an unfamiliar format gets flagged, not guessed at — which is exactly the kind of concrete limit a decision-maker needs.

contentSections.synthesis: Function, mechanism, limits — each is one plain sentence, and each does a job the others can't: the function sentence says why anyone should care, the mechanism sentence keeps it from sounding like magic, and the limits sentence keeps the whole explanation from becoming an accidental over-promise.

contentSections.title: Closing the loop back to the decision

contentSections.question: Put these four sentences in the order that makes a coherent ninety-second explanation for the partners meeting.
steps: It reads incoming client documents and fills in the fields our staff currently type by hand.
It's been shown examples of our real documents with correct fields marked, and learned to spot the same patterns in a new one.
On a format it hasn't seen a clear example of, it flags the document for a person instead of guessing.
That means less time on the document types we send it every season, with the harder or unusual ones staying exactly as reviewed as they are today.
contentSections.explanation: Function has to come first — it's what makes the room care enough to keep listening. Mechanism comes second, because it explains the function just stated, before any limits are introduced. Limits come third, once the room has a working idea of how it functions, so the boundary lands as a specific fact about a real thing rather than a vague warning about an unknown one. The close comes last because it can only make sense once all three previous facts are on the table — it's the sentence that turns three facts into a reason to act.

contentSections.body: A compressed explanation has a fixed shape — function, mechanism, limits, close — and each is one plain sentence. Skipping any one of them leaves the room with an inflated, confusing, or pointless picture.

title: Analogies that don't quietly mislead
description: Every common AI analogy gets something right and something wrong — the skill is naming both halves before using one, not picking whichever analogy sounds most reassuring.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a proposed analogy for what it accurately conveys and what it wrongly implies about accountability, process, or capability
Select or modify an analogy to fit the specific capability being explained

contentSections.body: In the partners meeting, someone asks: “so is this basically like a really smart intern reading the documents?” It's a natural question, reaching for something familiar. It's also an analogy with a specific, costly implication buried inside it: an intern learns from correction over time and can be held accountable for a mistake in a way that maps onto how the firm already manages people. The pipeline does neither of those things the way an intern does, and if that mismatch isn't named, the analogy quietly sets an expectation about how the system will improve and who's responsible when it doesn't.

Every common AI analogy has the same structure: it gets something real right, and it wrongly implies something else. **“A really smart intern”** rightly conveys that it's producing a first draft a person reviews — and wrongly implies ongoing, cumulative learning from correction and personal accountability, neither of which describes how a fixed model actually behaves between retraining cycles. **“Basically autocomplete”** rightly conveys that it's predicting likely next content from patterns — and wrongly implies something dumber and more mechanical than what's actually happening, which undersells its ability to handle genuinely novel document layouts. **“Like Google but smarter”** rightly conveys fast, on-demand answers to a question — and wrongly implies it's retrieving and citing a specific source the way a search result does, when in fact (without a retrieval system attached) it's generating an answer from learned patterns with no guaranteed source behind it.

The skill isn't picking the safest-sounding analogy — it's stating what an analogy gets right, and immediately naming what it wrongly implies, in the same breath, the way lesson 2 of the previous module paired an inclusion with its boundary.

contentSections.scenario: A partner says: “so it's basically like Google — you ask it something and it tells you the answer.”
contentSections.question: What does this analogy specifically get wrong about Corrigan's extraction pipeline?

options.label: It implies the answer is being retrieved from, and traceable to, a specific source document — the pipeline generates a structured output from learned patterns, without that same retrieval-and-citation behavior
It wrongly implies the pipeline is slower than a search engine
Nothing — this is actually an accurate comparison

feedback.no-citation: Correct. A search engine's core promise is a traceable source; the extraction pipeline's core mechanism is pattern-matched field extraction, with no equivalent 'here's exactly where this came from' guarantee unless that's specifically built in. That gap matters if anyone in the room assumes extracted fields are automatically source-traceable the way a search result is.
feedback.too-slow: Speed isn't the axis where this analogy actually breaks down — the mismatch is about traceability and sourcing, not response time.
feedback.not-wrong: It's not entirely wrong — fast, on-demand response is a real similarity — but 'not entirely wrong' isn't the same as safe to leave unqualified; the traceability gap is exactly the kind of thing that has to be named.

contentSections.concept: An analogy chosen for how reassuring it sounds, rather than for how precisely it maps, imports the analogy's whole shape into the listener's mental model — including the parts that don't actually apply.

contentSections.title: Fitting the analogy to the actual capability

contentSections.scenario: You're choosing how to describe the pipeline's behavior on a format it hasn't seen before — the specific limit named in lesson 1's build-it exercise.
contentSections.question: Select every statement that pairs an analogy with its accurate qualifier, the way this lesson teaches.

items.label: “Like a new hire's first draft — except it doesn't get better at handling an unfamiliar case just from being told once; that update happens on our schedule, not automatically”

“Like autocomplete, but working from patterns in whole documents rather than just the next word — which is why it can handle a document it's structurally never seen before, not just fill in an obvious blank”
“It's basically like having a new intern on the team”
“It's smart enough to figure most things out on its own”

explanation.intern-qualified: Applicable. This keeps the useful part of the intern comparison (a first draft a person reviews) while explicitly correcting the part that misleads (ongoing automatic learning from a single correction).
explanation.autocomplete-qualified: Applicable. This keeps the useful part (pattern-based prediction) while correcting the undersell (it's not just completing an obvious blank — it's working from whole-document structure).
explanation.intern-unqualified: Not applicable — this is the analogy stated without its correction, which is exactly the version that imports the misleading half along with the useful half.
explanation.magic-box: Not applicable, and worse than an unqualified analogy — it doesn't even gesture at a real mechanism, which fails the mechanism-sentence requirement from the previous lesson entirely.

contentSections.synthesis: A well-used analogy always arrives with its own correction attached — the useful half stated, and the misleading half named in the same breath. An analogy left bare, or replaced with a vague “it's smart,” imports whatever the listener's imagination fills in.

contentSections.body: Every common AI analogy is half right. Name what it gets right and what it wrongly implies, in the same breath — don't reach for whichever one sounds most reassuring and leave it unqualified.

title: Saying "it will sometimes be wrong" and still being hired
description: Admitting an error rate doesn't cost the engagement — an error rate stated without a mitigation plan does. The two together read as professional; the number alone reads as a warning sign.

learningObjectives.text: State a system's error rate alongside its mitigation plan, in a way that reads as competence rather than as a warning sign

contentSections.title: The number everyone's afraid to say out loud

contentSections.body: A junior colleague drafts the capability briefing for the partners and leaves out the pilot's actual number — the extraction pipeline gets fields right without a human fix on about 91% of standard documents. “If we say 9% wrong, they'll think it's broken,” he says. “Let's just say it's ‘highly accurate’ and leave it there.” It sounds like the safer version. It's the version most likely to blow up the first time a partner notices a wrong field in production and nobody warned them it would ever happen.

“It will sometimes be wrong” is not, on its own, disqualifying information to a room full of partners who run a business that also has an error rate — misfiled documents happen today, by hand, and everyone in the room already knows it. What actually damages trust isn't the number; it's a number with nothing attached to it, or no number at all replaced by a vague reassurance that later gets contradicted by a real mistake nobody was warned about.

The version that reads as professional pairs the number with what happens when it's wrong: “on standard documents, about 91% of fields come out correct without a fix — the remaining 9% get flagged, because low-confidence fields are routed to a person rather than silently guessed at, the same way an ambiguous case gets escalated today.” This sentence does three things a bare “highly accurate” doesn't: it gives a real number instead of a vague adjective, it explains the failure mode (flagged, not silent), and it ties the mitigation to something the room already trusts — the existing escalation habit.

contentSections.code:
Junior colleague's draft slide for the partners meeting:

“Corrigan's new AI intake system is highly accurate and will significantly reduce manual document handling.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this sentence, given the pilot's real 91% figure exists?

options.label: It replaces a real, known number with a vague adjective, and states no mitigation for the cases it gets wrong — leaving the room with no warning before the first visible error
91% isn't actually accurate enough to mention in a partners meeting
The sentence is too short to be a real capability statement

feedback.vague-no-mitigation: Correct. “Highly accurate” sounds reassuring and commits to nothing checkable — when the first wrong field shows up in production, nobody in the room was told to expect that, because the sentence never said it would happen or what happens when it does.
feedback.number-too-low: 91% is a strong, real result for a first release — the lesson isn't that the number is too low to mention, it's that hiding it behind a vague adjective is worse than stating it plainly alongside the mitigation.
feedback.too-short: Length isn't the issue — a short sentence can absolutely include the number and the mitigation; this one is short because it deliberately omits both, not because brevity itself is the flaw.

contentSections.flawExplanation: “Highly accurate” is a sentence built to sound safe, and it's actually the riskier choice — it sets no expectation for what a wrong field looks like or what happens to it, so the first real error in production arrives as a surprise instead of as the expected, planned-for 9% the pilot already measured.

contentSections.title: Pairing the number with the plan

contentSections.problem: Write the paired error-rate-and-mitigation sentence for Corrigan's pipeline, from the pilot's 91% figure.

steps.label: State the real number plainly
steps.work: “On standard documents — the W-2s, 1099s, and receipts from the pilot — about 91% of fields come out correct without a person fixing them.”
steps.why: A specific number, tied to a specific tested category, is checkable and concrete in a way “highly accurate” can never be — and it's the exact figure the honest pilot from the previous module exists to produce.

steps.label: State what happens to the other cases, specifically
steps.work: “The remaining fields get flagged for a person to check — the system doesn't guess on a low-confidence field, it routes it, the same way an ambiguous case gets escalated to Walt today.”
steps.why: This is the mitigation half — it tells the room exactly what a wrong or uncertain field looks like in practice, so a flagged item in production reads as the system working as designed, not as it breaking.

steps.label: Tie it back to something the room already trusts
steps.work: “That's the same escalation pattern the team already uses for anything unusual — this just adds a faster first pass in front of it.”
steps.why: Anchoring the new behavior to an existing, trusted habit is what keeps the number from sounding like a new risk — it's framed as the same safety net the firm already relies on, applied earlier in the process.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. The pilot also measured that on the hardest document type tested (handwritten receipts), only about 60% of fields come out correct without a fix. Write the paired sentence for this number.

blanks.prompt: State the real number plainly, tied to its specific category.
blanks.answer: On handwritten receipts specifically, about 60% of fields come out correct without a person fixing them — notably lower than the standard-document figure
accept: 60% correct on handwritten receipts, named as the weaker category
blanks.why: Naming the category explicitly, rather than blending it into an overall average, is exactly what the module-earlier lesson on per-type breakdowns warned against skipping.

blanks.prompt: State the mitigation for this weaker case.
blanks.answer: Handwritten receipts are flagged for full manual review by default, rather than routed only when a field is low-confidence — the system treats the whole category as needing a person, not just individual uncertain fields
accept: the whole category gets routed to manual review by default, not just uncertain fields within it
blanks.why: A weaker category needs a different, more conservative mitigation than the general flagging rule — stating that difference explicitly is what keeps the mitigation honest rather than reusing a reassurance that doesn't actually fit this case.

blanks.prompt: Tie it back to something the room trusts.
blanks.answer: This is treated the same way a genuinely illegible document is handled today — set aside for a person from the start, rather than guessed at
accept: handled the same way an illegible document is already handled manually today
blanks.why: Anchoring even a weaker result to an existing, already-trusted habit keeps a lower number from reading as a new, unmanaged risk.

faded.procedure: For any category's number, state it plainly and specifically, state the actual mitigation for that category (which may differ by category, as the weak-case version shows), and anchor the mitigation to something the room already trusts.

contentSections.body: The error rate isn't the risk — an error rate with no mitigation attached is. State the real number, state what happens to the rest, and anchor it to a habit the room already trusts.

title: Writing for the person who forwards your email upward
description: A capability email written for the sponsor who understands the context gets forwarded, unedited, to people who don't — the explanation has to hold up for a reader with zero shared history with the project.

learningObjectives.text: Rewrite an explanation that depends on shared context into one that holds up for a reader with none
Identify the specific phrases in a draft that only make sense to someone already in the conversation

contentSections.title: The email that leaves the room without you

contentSections.body: Denise emails after the meeting: “this is great, mind if I forward it to the full partner board? A few of them couldn't make it today.” The email being forwarded was written for Denise — someone who sat through the kickoff, saw the demo, and already knows what “the pilot” and “the format inventory” refer to. The partners who couldn't make it today will read the identical words with none of that. The email either explains itself, or it doesn't, and there's no consultant in the room to fill the gap this time.

Writing for the forward means treating every email that might travel beyond its original recipient as if it will — because once it's sent, that decision isn't the consultant's to make anymore. Two specific things go wrong when this isn't done deliberately: **unexplained shorthand** (“the pilot went well” means nothing to someone who wasn't told what the pilot tested or why), and **assumed context** (“as discussed” or “per our conversation” references a conversation the new reader wasn't part of, and reads as a locked door rather than a link).

The fix isn't writing a longer email for everyone in case they forward it — it's writing the specific email for the sponsor with an eye toward the version that would still make sense stripped of everything sitting in your own head and Denise's. A sentence like “the pilot went well” becomes “we tested the pipeline against a full, unfiltered week of real client documents — the harder ones included — and it correctly filled in 91% of fields without anyone needing to fix them.” The second version doesn't require having been in the room.

contentSections.problem: Rewrite this sentence from Denise's briefing email so it holds up for a partner who wasn't at the kickoff or the demo: “Following up on the pilot — results were strong, and as discussed, the next phase is the format extension.”

steps.label: Identify the shorthand and the assumed context
steps.work: “The pilot” (what was tested, on what, measuring what?), “results were strong” (compared to what, specifically?), “as discussed” (discussed with whom, when, about what?), and “the format extension” (extension of what, to what?) are all doing work only for someone who was in the earlier conversations.
steps.why: Naming each vague phrase specifically is what makes it possible to fix — a general sense that the email is 'too insider' isn't actionable the way a list of specific unexplained phrases is.

steps.label: Replace each with a self-contained version
steps.work: “We tested the document-intake pipeline against a full week of real client documents, hard cases included. It correctly filled in 91% of fields without anyone needing to fix them — the rest were flagged for a person to check, the same way an unusual case is handled today. The next phase adds support for document types the pilot didn't cover yet, like the scanned mileage logs from trucking clients.”
steps.why: Each replacement states what would otherwise require having been in the room — what was tested, what the number actually means, and what 'next phase' refers to — so the paragraph is complete on its own.

steps.label: Check it against a reader with zero context
steps.work: Read the rewritten paragraph as if seeing it for the first time, with no memory of any kickoff or demo — does every noun (“the pipeline,” “the pilot,” “a person,” “the next phase”) resolve to something explained earlier in the same email?
steps.why: This check is what catches a remaining gap before the email is sent — it's cheap to do and it's the difference between an email that survives being forwarded and one that generates a confused reply-all.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. Rewrite: “Quick update — Walt's on board now, and the demo covered the usual suspects. Full rollout's still on track.”

blanks.prompt: Identify the shorthand and assumed context in this sentence.
blanks.answer: 'Walt's on board' assumes the reader knows who Walt is and that there was ever a question of his buy-in; 'the usual suspects' assumes the reader knows which document types those are; 'full rollout' and 'on track' give no sense of what rollout means or what 'track' it's being measured against
accept: Walt's identity/role, what 'usual suspects' refers to, and what 'rollout' and 'on track' concretely mean are all unexplained
blanks.why: Each of these phrases is a compressed reference to a shared history the new reader doesn't have — naming them individually is what makes each one fixable.

blanks.prompt: Write the self-contained replacement.
blanks.answer: 'Walt Sorensen, Corrigan's senior tax reviewer, has reviewed the pipeline's output directly and is comfortable with how flagged items are routed to him. The demo covered the standard document types — W-2s, 1099s, and typical receipts. We're on schedule for the full rollout, targeted for [date], covering those standard types first.'
accept: a version that names who Walt is, what document types were covered, and what the rollout date/target actually is
blanks.why: Each shorthand phrase is replaced with the specific fact it was standing in for, so the sentence carries its own meaning without requiring the reader to already know Walt, the document list, or the schedule.

faded.procedure: For any email that might travel beyond its original recipient: list every phrase that only makes sense with shared context, replace each with a self-contained version naming the specific fact, and read the result as a stranger to check nothing still depends on having been in the room.

contentSections.title: Spotting the gap before it's sent

contentSections.body: Once an email leaves your outbox, whether it stays with the original reader isn't your decision anymore. Write it so it holds up for whoever it actually reaches — assume the forward, not the exception.

title: Handling the executive who read one article
description: An executive citing one impressive headline isn't wrong about what they read — they're missing the gap between a benchmark result and production reliability on this firm's actual messy documents, and the fix is engaging that gap directly, not dismissing the article.

learningObjectives.text: Respond to a benchmark-based challenge by distinguishing benchmark performance from production reliability on the client's own data, without dismissing the premise

contentSections.title: The article that's true and beside the point

contentSections.body: Greg Voss, a partner who wasn't at the kickoff, read an article over the weekend: “AI passes the CPA exam.” In the meeting he asks, not unreasonably: “if it can pass the CPA exam, why do we need six weeks and a whole team to read some W-2s?” The article is real and the claim in it is true. It's also not a claim about anything Corrigan is actually trying to do, and dismissing Greg's question outright — or worse, agreeing that six weeks now sounds unnecessary — both handle this worse than engaging with what the article actually showed.

The instinct to either dismiss the article (“that's not really relevant”) or awkwardly concede ground (“well, maybe we could go faster”) both skip the actual, answerable question underneath Greg's challenge: what does “passing an exam” have in common with, and what does it leave out of, “correctly reading Corrigan's actual documents”?

A CPA exam is a fixed, clean, well-formatted set of standardized questions with known right answers, taken once. Corrigan's actual documents are inconsistent scans, phone photos, faxes, and handwriting, arriving continuously, all season, where a wrong answer becomes a real number on a real return. The article's claim is true and it's about performance on the exam's specific format — it says nothing about performance on Corrigan's specific documents, which is exactly what the pilot in this module's earlier lessons exists to measure instead of assume.

The response that actually engages Greg's question: agree with what's true in the premise, name the specific gap between exam performance and Corrigan's production reality, and point to the pilot's actual number as the honest answer to what Greg really wants to know.

contentSections.title: Answering Greg without dismissing or conceding
Greg pushes back live
contentSections.opening: Greg, having asked his question, doesn't drop it: “okay, but that just sounds like an excuse for a slow timeline. If it's that capable, what's actually taking six weeks?”

pushback.situation: The room is watching how this gets handled.
pushback.question: What's the strongest response?

choices.label: “You're right, we can probably move faster — let's compress the timeline”
choices.consequence: This concedes a real, tested reason (unvalidated performance on Corrigan's own hard documents) in exchange for looking responsive — and it recreates exactly the over-promise this whole track has been warning against, based on nothing more than social pressure in the room.

choices.label: “That article isn't really relevant to what we're doing”
choices.consequence: This is technically defensible and lands badly — it sounds like brushing off a partner's legitimate question rather than engaging with it, and it doesn't actually explain anything to Greg or the rest of the room.

choices.label: “Passing the exam means it's good at clean, standardized questions with known answers. Six weeks is building and testing against Corrigan's actual messy documents — we already measured 91% accuracy on the standard ones and found the real gap is handwritten receipts, which is specifically what the remaining weeks address”
choices.consequence: This agrees with what's true, names the specific and real difference, and backs it with the pilot's actual number — Greg gets a real, checkable answer instead of either a concession or a brush-off.

conceded.summary: The timeline gets compressed based on social pressure, not on what the pilot actually found about handwritten receipts — the exact risk this module's expectations-setting lessons were built to prevent resurfaces here, driven by an executive's misapplied benchmark instead of an unaddressed remark.
conceded.lesson: A benchmark headline is not evidence about production performance on this client's own documents — conceding to it under social pressure reintroduces the identical risk that a proper pilot exists to rule out.

dismissed.summary: Greg isn't wrong that the article is impressive, and being told it's 'not relevant' with no explanation reads as evasive rather than informed — he's left with an unanswered question and a reasonable suspicion that his challenge was brushed off rather than addressed.
dismissed.lesson: Dismissing a partner's premise without explaining why doesn't win the argument — it just removes the chance to actually inform the room.

engaged.summary: Greg gets a specific, checkable answer: what the benchmark actually measures, what Corrigan's documents actually require, and the real number from the pilot that shows exactly where the gap is. The timeline holds because it's now grounded in a measured fact, not an assumption either way.
engaged.lesson: The strongest response to a benchmark-based challenge agrees with what's true, names the specific gap to this client's real situation, and answers with a measured number rather than a general reassurance.

contentSections.body: An executive citing an impressive article isn't wrong about the article — engage the real gap between what it measured and what your pilot measured, backed by your own number, instead of dismissing the premise or conceding the timeline.

title: Practice — Rewrite Seven Technical Explanations for a Sponsor
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given a jargon-heavy or over-promising explanation, apply this module's compression, analogy, and error-rate skills.

learningObjectives.text: Rewrite technical explanations for a non-technical sponsor using the function/mechanism/limits/close structure
Identify unqualified analogies and hidden error-rate omissions in draft explanations

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing is timed, and the set doesn't expire — do all seven now or split them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the lab — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Write and Test a Capability Briefing on a Real Reader
description: Write a one-page capability briefing for a new client's non-technical board, test it on an actual reader, and record specifically what they got wrong on the first draft.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a one-page capability briefing using the function/mechanism/limits/close structure and a checked analogy
Diagnose specific misunderstandings a real reader had from a first draft, and revise to close them

contentSections.body: Solano Behavioral Health Group's founder, Dr. Renata Ibarra, needs a one-page briefing for her practice's advisory board — five therapists with no technical background, none of whom were part of the earlier scoping or kickoff. This lab writes that briefing and tests it the way this module argues it should be tested: on an actual reader, not just reread by its own author.

contentSections.title: A tested capability briefing
contentSections.brief: Write a one-page briefing on the session-note drafting tool for Solano's advisory board, covering the compressed explanation structure, a checked analogy, and the honest error rate with mitigation. Then have a real person read it cold (a friend, family member, or colleague unfamiliar with the project) and record exactly what they misunderstood or asked about.
contentSections.deliverable: The one-page briefing, plus a short write-up of what your test reader got wrong or asked about on the first draft, and the specific revision made in response to each.

stages.title: Write the ninety-second explanation core
stages.instructions: Write the function/mechanism/limits/close for the session-note tool: reads a therapist's spoken summary, drafts a first-pass note from learned patterns in past approved notes, never finalizes or submits without review, and connects to what the advisory board actually needs to decide (approving the pilot).
stages.checkpoint: You have one plain sentence for each of the four elements, in order.

stages.title: Choose and qualify an analogy
stages.instructions: Pick one analogy for this tool and pair it explicitly with what it wrongly implies, the way this module's lessons modeled.
stages.checkpoint: The analogy sentence names both what it gets right and what it wrongly implies, in the same breath.

stages.title: Write the error rate and mitigation, and assemble the full page
stages.instructions: Invent a plausible pilot figure (e.g. a percentage of draft notes accepted with only minor edits) and pair it with a specific mitigation, then assemble the full one-page briefing with all elements, written to hold up for a reader who wasn't in any earlier conversation.
stages.checkpoint: The briefing includes a specific number, a specific mitigation, and no unexplained shorthand.

stages.title: Test it on a real reader and revise
stages.instructions: Have someone unfamiliar with the project read the briefing cold. Ask what they think it does, what they think its limits are, and what confused them. Record their actual answers, then revise the briefing to close whatever gap they revealed.
stages.checkpoint: You have specific, recorded misunderstandings from a real reader, and a revision addressing each one.

rubric.criterion: The explanation follows function/mechanism/limits/close, each as a single plain sentence
rubric.meets: All four elements are present, in order, without technical jargon.

rubric.criterion: The analogy is qualified, not left bare
rubric.meets: The write-up states both what the analogy gets right and what it wrongly implies.

rubric.criterion: The error rate is real and paired with a specific mitigation
rubric.meets: A number is stated (even if invented for this exercise) alongside what happens to the cases it misses.

rubric.criterion: The briefing holds up with no unexplained shorthand
rubric.meets: Every reference resolves within the document itself, with nothing depending on outside context.

rubric.criterion: The test reader's actual reaction is recorded and used
rubric.meets: At least one genuine misunderstanding or question from a real reader is named, with the specific revision made in response.

contentSections.body: A briefing that reads clearly to its author isn't the same as one that reads clearly to a stranger — testing it on an actual reader is what turns an assumption of clarity into a checked one.

title: Checkpoint — Explaining AI to People Who Don't Care How It Works
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous module, two from three modules back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's explanation-structure and analogy distinctions, and earlier modules' expectation-setting and scoping distinctions, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Explaining AI to People Who Don't Care How It Works

questions.from: This module — Explaining AI to People Who Don't Care How It Works
questions.prompt: A compressed capability explanation has four elements in a fixed order. What are they?

options.label: Function, mechanism, limits, close
History, technology, pricing, competitors
Mechanism only — the other details can be skipped in ninety seconds

questions.explanation: Function comes first to earn attention, mechanism explains it without jargon, limits state the boundary plainly, and the close connects all three to the actual decision at hand.

questions.from: This module — Explaining AI to People Who Don't Care How It Works
questions.prompt: Why does skipping the mechanism sentence specifically cause a problem?

options.label: It leaves the capability sounding like magic, which triggers either suspicion or over-trust
It makes the explanation too short to be useful
It has no real effect either way

questions.explanation: A capability with no stated mechanism reads as unexplainable, which pushes listeners toward either distrust or uncritical over-trust — neither of which is the accurate, grounded picture the explanation is meant to produce.

questions.from: This module — Explaining AI to People Who Don't Care How It Works
questions.prompt: A partner calls the pipeline “basically like Google.” What does this specifically get wrong?

options.label: It implies the answer is retrieved from and traceable to a specific source, when the pipeline generates structured output from learned patterns without that same guarantee
It wrongly implies the pipeline is slower than a search engine
Nothing — it's an accurate comparison

questions.explanation: The mismatch is about source traceability, not speed — a search result points at a specific source; the pipeline's output doesn't carry that same guarantee unless retrieval is specifically built in.

questions.from: This module — Explaining AI to People Who Don't Care How It Works
questions.prompt: What makes a used analogy safe, per this module?

options.label: Stating what it gets right and what it wrongly implies, in the same breath
Choosing whichever analogy sounds most reassuring to the room
Avoiding analogies entirely and using only technical language

questions.explanation: A qualified analogy keeps the useful comparison while correcting the part that would otherwise mislead — an unqualified reassuring analogy imports its whole shape, including the wrong parts.

questions.from: Previous module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: Priya proposes a pilot using only 15 clean, complete documents. What's the actual flaw?

options.label: The sample deliberately excludes hard cases, so it can't answer how the pipeline handles Corrigan's real document mix
15 documents is too few to be statistically valid
The results shouldn't be shown at a partner meeting

questions.explanation: The flaw is selection, not count — a sample chosen to exclude the hard cases produces a number that can't speak to real production performance.

questions.from: Previous module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: Why does a written kickoff recap actually prevent a later dispute, rather than just documenting one?

options.label: It gives both sides a shared, dated reference, so a disagreement becomes a lookup instead of a contest of two memories
It legally binds every word spoken in the kickoff
It doesn't prevent anything, only documents after the fact

questions.explanation: The value is a shared, neutral, dated reference — pointing back to a record is fundamentally different from each side reciting a memory of the call.

questions.from: Previous module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: Why can a demo showing only genuinely true, unscripted results still mislead an audience?

options.label: A demo can only show a slice, and an audience tends to assume that slice represents the whole
It can't mislead if every individual claim is accurate
Only scripted demos can mislead

questions.explanation: The risk isn't in any individual claim being false — it's in the gap between what a short demo can show and what production actually is, which an audience's imagination tends to fill in optimistically.

questions.from: Previous module — Setting Expectations That Hold
questions.prompt: What's the difference between proactive negative-scoping and reactive correction?

options.label: Proactive scoping states a boundary before anyone assumes otherwise; reactive correction only responds after a gap-revealing remark
They're the same technique under two names
Reactive correction is always preferable since it responds to a real signal

questions.explanation: Proactive scoping states the boundary in the same breath as the inclusion, before an assumption forms — reactive correction only exists to clean up after one already has.

questions.from: Three modules back — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: A vague one-sentence enquiry like “help with tax season” — what's the first job, before proposing anything?

options.label: Enumerate the plausible distinct projects it could mean, and ask questions that tell them apart
Propose the most common AI product for the client's industry
Ask for a budget number immediately

questions.explanation: A vague enquiry names a feeling, not a task — the first job is separating the plausible projects it could mean before proposing any single one.

questions.from: Three modules back — Scoping and Pricing
questions.prompt: What's the actual purpose of a priced discovery phase in a hybrid pricing structure?

options.label: To convert an unmeasured range into a written inventory, on a small bounded budget, before a fixed price is attached to the build
To give the consultant extra billable hours before the real work starts
To delay the client from asking about price

questions.explanation: A discovery phase turns an unknown range into a counted, written inventory on a small fixed budget, so the build's fixed price rests on something real instead of a guess.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Resistance is usually information
description: Treating resistance as an obstacle to route around throws away the most specific, situated knowledge available about why an automation might actually fail — reading it as information is what makes it useful instead of just inconvenient.

learningObjectives.text: Reframe an instance of resistance as a specific, investigable concern rather than an obstacle to route around

contentSections.body: Three weeks into the extraction pipeline's rollout, Walt Sorensen keeps “forgetting” to run his queue's documents through the new system before doing them the old way. He's not hostile about it, and he's not raising it as a formal objection — he just quietly doesn't use it, week after week, while saying it looks “fine” whenever Denise asks. The easy read is that Walt is resistant to change, twenty-five years into the job, and the plan is to route around him — get everyone else using it and let adoption pressure bring him along eventually.

That read treats resistance as a personality trait to be waited out. A more useful read treats it as data: Walt, more than almost anyone else at Corrigan, has direct, specific knowledge of exactly which documents go wrong and how — because catching them by hand is what he's been doing for twenty-five years. His quiet non-use isn't necessarily stubbornness; it might be an accurate, if unstated, signal that something about the new system doesn't yet hold up against the cases he specifically knows are dangerous to miss.

Routing around resistance treats the resister as the obstacle. Reading resistance as information treats the resistance itself as a symptom worth diagnosing — the same move this whole track has taught for a vague client enquiry, a stray unscoped remark, or a demo that landed too well. The question isn't “how do we get Walt to comply,” it's “what does Walt know that the pipeline doesn't yet account for.”

contentSections.scenario: Instead of assuming Walt is simply resistant to change, you ask him directly, in a low-pressure one-on-one: “what's making you want to double-check everything by hand still?” He says: “last time we brought in a system, it looked fine in the demo and then missed something on a return with an out-of-state rental property — I caught it by luck, not because the system flagged it.”
contentSections.question: What does Walt's answer reveal that a 'he's just resistant to change' read would have missed entirely?

options.label: A specific prior failure mode — a real category of case (out-of-state rental property returns) the last system missed — that's directly relevant to testing this one
Nothing new — Walt is simply a cautious person by nature, which was already assumed
That Walt is primarily worried about losing his job

feedback.specific-prior-failure: Correct. Walt's answer names a specific, checkable category of case that failed before — exactly the kind of edge case a pilot needs to be tested against, and something nobody would have known to test for without asking Walt directly.
feedback.just-cautious-by-nature: This ignores the actual content of his answer — he didn't describe a general disposition, he described a specific incident with a specific case type, which is exactly the useful information a 'he's just cautious' read discards.
feedback.wants-job-security: Nothing in this specific answer is about job security — that's a real and separate concern worth checking (covered later in this module), but reading every instance of resistance as the same underlying fear misses what Walt actually said here.

contentSections.mechanism: A specific, investigated reason behind resistance is almost always more useful than the resistance itself — it either surfaces a real gap worth fixing (as here) or reveals a different, equally real concern (like job security) that needs its own, different response. Assuming the reason without asking collapses both possibilities into “stubbornness,” which points toward no useful action at all.

contentSections.title: What routing around it actually costs

contentSections.scenario: A colleague argues for the “route around Walt” plan: get everyone else on board, let usage pressure bring him along. Weigh what this plan actually risks.
contentSections.question: Select every real risk in routing around Walt's resistance instead of investigating it.

items.label: If Walt's non-use is signaling a real, uncaught failure mode, it stays uncaught until it surfaces in production instead of in testing
Walt's twenty-five years of specific edge-case knowledge never gets incorporated into the pilot's test set
Adoption pressure might get Walt to technically use the tool without ever resolving whatever the actual concern was
Routing around Walt is genuinely faster than a one-on-one conversation, so it's worth the tradeoff

explanation.miss-real-gap: Applicable. If the out-of-state-rental case type genuinely isn't handled well, waiting it out means finding that out from a real production mistake instead of from Walt's warning.
explanation.lose-expertise: Applicable. Walt's specific, hard-won knowledge of exactly where things go wrong is a resource — the plan to route around him actively discards it instead of using it.
explanation.adoption-pressure-doesnt-fix-content: Applicable. Getting Walt to use the tool under peer pressure doesn't make the out-of-state-rental case handling any better — it just makes an unresolved concern invisible instead of resolved.
explanation.faster-overall: Not applicable — a single fifteen-minute conversation with Walt is cheap, and the potential cost of a missed edge case in production is not a small tradeoff to make in exchange for skipping it.

contentSections.synthesis: Routing around resistance doesn't make the underlying concern go away — it just removes the chance to find out whether the concern was pointing at something real, at exactly the moment (before rollout, not after) when finding out is cheap.

contentSections.body: Resistance is usually information, not an obstacle — the person quietly not using the new system often knows something specific and real that the system doesn't yet account for. Ask before routing around.

title: The person who knows why the last attempt failed
