description: Someone who lived through a previous failed rollout carries institutional knowledge no document captured — treating them as a source to learn from, deliberately, beats dismissing their skepticism as baggage.

learningObjectives.text: Extract specific, actionable institutional knowledge from a person who experienced a previous failed attempt at similar work

contentSections.body: The out-of-state-rental-property incident Walt mentioned turns out to trace back to a practice-management software rollout Corrigan tried eight years ago — a system that was supposed to auto-flag unusual return types and never did, quietly, for most of a season, until Walt caught the pattern by hand. There's no written record of this. It lives entirely in Walt's memory, and in whatever caution it left him with about the next system that promises to catch things automatically.

A failed rollout eight years ago, with nobody documenting exactly what went wrong or why, doesn't disappear from the organization — it survives as an unwritten caution in whoever was there for it, usually expressed as skepticism rather than as a structured lesson. Dismissing that skepticism as “Walt's just been burned before, he'll come around” treats the caution as baggage to wait out, the same mistake as treating resistance as a personality trait rather than data.

The alternative is treating Walt deliberately as a source: asking specifically what the old system was supposed to do, specifically what it actually did, and specifically what the gap between those two things looked like in practice. That's not a therapy conversation about his feelings toward new systems — it's an interview aimed at recovering institutional knowledge that exists nowhere else, the organizational equivalent of Halsted's undocumented broker-template drift from an earlier phase of this track: real, costly information that only survives in one person's memory unless someone deliberately asks for it.

contentSections.problem: Structure the interview with Walt to extract the specific, actionable lessons from the eight-year-old failed rollout.

steps.label: Ask what the old system was supposed to do, in Walt's own words
steps.work: “What was it actually supposed to catch — walk me through what you were told it would do.”
steps.why: Starting with the promise, not the failure, gets an accurate baseline for what 'failed' even means here — without it, 'it didn't work' has no specific shape.

steps.label: Ask what it actually did, with specific examples
steps.work: “And what did it actually flag, versus what you found by hand? Walk me through the out-of-state-rental case specifically.”
steps.why: Specific examples are what turn a general impression (“it missed things”) into a checkable, testable category — the same specificity a pilot's own test set needs, from the person who has it firsthand.

steps.label: Ask what, if anything, would have caught it
steps.work: “Looking back, is there something specific that could have caught that case — a rule, a flag, a review step — that wasn't there?”
steps.why: This turns the retrospective into forward-looking, actionable input: not just 'here's what went wrong' but 'here's what a working version would specifically need to do differently.'

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. Walt also mentions the old system's onboarding was “basically a fifteen-minute video and that was it” — apply the same interview structure to this second thread.

blanks.prompt: What was the old system's onboarding supposed to accomplish, in Walt's words?
blanks.answer: Get staff comfortable enough to trust the system's flags and know what to do when something came up flagged
accept: prepare staff to use and trust the new flagging behavior
blanks.why: Establishing what onboarding was meant to achieve gives a real baseline for judging whether a fifteen-minute video actually achieved it.

blanks.prompt: What actually happened, specifically?
blanks.answer: Staff watched the video once, mostly forgot the specifics within weeks, and fell back on old manual habits because nobody reinforced the new process after the initial video
accept: the training didn't stick, and staff reverted to old habits without reinforcement
blanks.why: The specific failure (no reinforcement, not just a bad video) is what's actually actionable for the current rollout's training plan.

blanks.prompt: What would Walt say could have prevented this specific onboarding failure?
blanks.answer: Some kind of follow-up check-in or refresher a few weeks in, not just a one-time video with no reinforcement
accept: a follow-up or refresher after the initial training, rather than a single one-time session
blanks.why: This is directly actionable input for how training should actually be structured this time — a specific, testable improvement, not a vague 'do better' impression.

faded.procedure: For any prior failed attempt someone lived through: ask what it was supposed to do, ask what actually happened with specific examples, and ask what — specifically — might have prevented it. The output is a short list of concrete, testable design requirements, not a general sense that 'the last one didn't go well.'

contentSections.title: Turning Walt's history into the current pilot's design

contentSections.question: Put these in the order that turns Walt's institutional knowledge into an actual improvement to the current pipeline's pilot.
steps: Interview Walt specifically about what the old system was supposed to do, what it actually did, and what would have caught the gap
Add the out-of-state-rental-property case, and similar unusual return types, explicitly to the pilot's test set
Add a follow-up check-in a few weeks after initial training, addressing the onboarding gap he named
Report back to Walt specifically what changed because of what he said
contentSections.explanation: The interview has to happen first, since it's the source of everything that follows. Adding the specific case type to the test set is the direct, technical translation of what he described. Adding the follow-up check-in addresses the second thread he raised, about onboarding. Reporting back to Walt closes the loop — without it, from Walt's side, this looks identical to the “vent to someone and nothing changes” pattern he may have already lived through once, and that closing step is what actually earns trust rather than just extracting information from him.

contentSections.body: The person who lived through the last failed attempt is carrying institutional knowledge that exists nowhere else. Interview them deliberately for specifics, then show them what changed because of what they said.

title: Job-loss fear, spoken and unspoken
description: Job-loss fear doesn't always announce itself as job-loss fear — vague reassurance addressed to a fear that was never named out loud usually isn't trusted, because it never actually engaged with what's really being worried about.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when apparent process objections are functioning as a proxy for unspoken job-loss fear
Address job-loss fear directly and specifically rather than with a general reassurance

contentSections.title: The objection that isn't really about the objection

contentSections.body: Two of Corrigan's three seasonal preparers — hired every January through April specifically to help with the return-drafting crunch — have started raising oddly specific process objections about the pipeline: “what if it double-counts a deduction,” “what if it doesn't handle a state we don't usually see.” The concerns sound technical. Neither preparer has actually said the sentence that's almost certainly underneath them: if this tool gets good enough at first-pass drafting, will Corrigan still need three seasonal preparers next year?

Job-loss fear frequently doesn't announce itself directly — saying “I'm worried this will replace me” out loud, to the person implementing the thing, is a genuinely hard sentence to say, especially for seasonal staff with the least job security in the room already. It tends to surface instead as a stream of specific, technically-framed process objections that never quite land anywhere, because answering each one technically doesn't touch the actual concern generating them.

A general reassurance — “don't worry, this isn't about replacing anyone” — offered without being asked, to a fear that was never spoken, usually isn't trusted, for the same reason a vague “we'll do our best” exclusion isn't trusted: it doesn't reference anything specific enough to check. The more effective move is naming the likely unspoken concern directly and specifically: “I want to check something — is part of what's behind these questions a worry about what this means for next season's hiring? That's a completely reasonable thing to wonder, and here's what I actually know about the plan.” Naming it directly gives the fear somewhere to go, rather than leaving it to keep generating one more technical objection.

contentSections.scenario: A different preparer, Marcus, asks a highly specific process question in a team meeting: “does the tool automatically apply the standard deduction, or does someone still choose that manually?”
contentSections.question: How should this question be read, given the context of the two other preparers' recent pattern?

options.label: As a genuine, specific technical question about the process — worth answering directly and specifically on its own terms first
As definitely job-loss fear in disguise, regardless of content
As irrelevant to the pattern, since it's phrased differently from the other two questions

feedback.genuine-technical: Correct. Not every specific process question is a proxy for something else — this one is answerable and useful on its own terms. Reading every question as secretly about job security risks dismissing a real technical concern, which is its own kind of unhelpful over-reading.
feedback.always-job-fear: Treating every specific question as automatically disguised fear is its own error — it risks answering a real technical question with an unasked-for reassurance about job security, which can land as presumptuous or even alarming if that wasn't what the person meant.
feedback.ignore-context: The context matters for staying alert to the broader pattern, but that doesn't mean every individual question within it should be assumed to be about the same thing — each one still deserves to be evaluated on its own content first.

contentSections.concept: Reading resistance as information doesn't mean assuming every specific question is secretly about something else — it means staying alert to a genuine pattern (recurring, oddly specific process objections with no direct ask) while still answering each individual question honestly on its own terms.

contentSections.code:
Draft message to the preparer team (junior colleague's version):

“Just a reminder that this tool is here to help everyone, not replace anyone — no need to worry about your jobs!”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in sending this, unprompted, to the whole team?

options.label: It's a blanket reassurance addressed to a fear nobody officially raised, offered without being asked and without anything specific to check it against — which can read as either dismissive or, worse, as confirmation that job security really is a live concern worth worrying about
The message shouldn't have been sent to the whole team, only privately to the two preparers who asked specific questions
Reassuring people about their jobs is never appropriate for a consultant to do

feedback.unprompted-vague-reassurance: Correct. An unprompted, vague reassurance with nothing specific behind it can backfire in exactly the way over-reassurance always does — it can read as "why are they bringing this up unless it's actually a real risk," which is the opposite of the intended effect.
feedback.wrong-audience: Audience isn't really the core problem here — even sent privately to just the two preparers, the same vague, unprompted, unspecific reassurance would carry the same risk of backfiring.
feedback.never-appropriate: Addressing job-loss concerns honestly is a real and appropriate part of this work when the concern is genuinely there — the problem with this message isn't that the topic was raised, it's how vaguely and unpromptedly it was raised.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A reassurance this vague, sent to a fear that was never spoken out loud, doesn't resolve anything — it can't, because there's nothing specific in it to check against. The fix isn't avoiding the topic; it's the direct, specific version from the text section: naming the likely concern out loud, in a real conversation, with whatever specific facts are actually available about hiring plans.

contentSections.body: Job-loss fear often surfaces as a stream of technical objections rather than as itself. Naming the likely unspoken concern directly, with whatever specific facts are actually available, gives it somewhere real to go — a vague, unprompted reassurance usually doesn't.

title: Sponsors, users and the gap between them
description: The sponsor who commissions a project and the users whose daily work it changes often want genuinely different things — a consultant who only reports to the sponsor is optimizing for approval, not for a system anyone actually uses.

learningObjectives.text: Identify where a sponsor's stated goal and users' actual daily-work concerns diverge
Work both the sponsor relationship and the user relationship deliberately, rather than treating the sponsor as the only real client

contentSections.body: Denise Marsh, the sponsor, wants faster document intake and, eventually, real margin improvement from reduced review time — that's what she's judging the engagement against, per this phase's earlier expectations-setting work. Walt and the preparers, the actual users, want a tool that doesn't create a scary new failure mode on the cases that matter most, and that doesn't quietly threaten their jobs. Both are legitimate. They are not the same goal, and a rollout that only satisfies Denise's definition of success can still fail completely on the ground.

A sponsor typically judges an automation by outcomes they can see from a distance — time saved, cost reduced, a metric moving in the right direction. Users judge it by what changes about their actual daily work — whether it makes their job easier or harder, whether it's trustworthy on the cases they personally know are risky, whether it threatens their position. A consultant who only reports to the sponsor and treats user concerns as something to manage rather than something to solve is optimizing for the wrong signal: sponsor approval is necessary but not sufficient, because a tool nobody actually trusts or uses well doesn't produce the sponsor's outcome either — it just produces the appearance of adoption on a status report.

Working both relationships deliberately means treating Walt's edge-case concerns and the preparers' unspoken job-security worry as inputs to the actual design, the way lessons 1 through 3 of this module modeled, not as a separate “change management” problem to be handled with an all-hands email after the real technical work is done. It also means being honest with Denise when a user concern reveals something the sponsor's view genuinely couldn't see from a distance — like the out-of-state-rental-property case type, which Denise had no way of knowing about until Walt's resistance surfaced it.

contentSections.title: Reporting the gap honestly to the sponsor

contentSections.scenario: Reporting progress to Denise, you have to decide what to include about Walt's concerns and the preparers' unspoken worry.
contentSections.question: Select every item that belongs in an honest status update to Denise, given what this module's earlier lessons found.

items.label: That Walt's resistance surfaced a real, previously untested case type (out-of-state rental properties) now added to the pilot's test set
That the eight-year-old rollout's onboarding failure pointed to a specific fix (a follow-up check-in) now built into this rollout's training plan
That some preparer questions may reflect an unspoken concern about next season's hiring, worth Denise being aware of as she plans staffing communication
A description of Walt as personally difficult or resistant to change, without the specific finding attached

explanation.edge-case-finding: Applicable. This is genuinely useful, specific information that came from investigating resistance rather than routing around it — exactly the kind of finding a sponsor needs to know about.
explanation.training-gap-finding: Applicable. A concrete design improvement traced to a real, named cause is valuable status information, not an unnecessary detail.
explanation.job-fear-pattern: Applicable, handled carefully — flagging the pattern (without naming individuals in a way that could feel like reporting on them) gives Denise useful context for how she communicates about staffing, which is ultimately her call to make, not the consultant's.
explanation.walt-named-personally: Not applicable. Describing Walt as 'resistant' without the specific finding attached reduces him to a personality trait in the report — exactly the framing this module opened by rejecting, and it also strips out the actually useful information (the edge case he found).

contentSections.synthesis: An honest status update translates what was learned from working with users into specific, useful information for the sponsor — findings and fixes, not personality judgments about the people who surfaced them.

contentSections.body: A sponsor's approval and a user's actual trust are different things, and only satisfying one of them doesn't produce a working rollout. Work both relationships deliberately, and report what users' concerns actually revealed — honestly, and specifically — back to the sponsor.

title: When the politics make the project undeliverable
description: Sometimes the honest finding is that the project, as currently framed, can't be delivered — recognizing that and saying so professionally is a real consulting skill, not a failure to manage the relationship.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when a political situation, not a technical one, makes a project undeliverable as currently framed
Name an undeliverable situation to the sponsor professionally, with options, rather than either forcing ahead or quietly disengaging

contentSections.title: When investigating resistance reveals something worse

contentSections.body: Following up privately with Priya, a harder fact surfaces: Denise has, in a separate conversation Priya wasn't supposed to repeat but felt was important, mentioned wanting the pipeline to eventually make it possible to run tax season with two fewer seasonal hires. Publicly, Denise has been saying, including to the preparers directly, that this project “isn't about replacing anyone.” Those two things aren't the same statement, and the preparers' unspoken job-fear from lesson 3 wasn't paranoia — it was accurate.

Every technique in this module up to now assumes the underlying situation is workable once the real concerns are surfaced and addressed — Walt's edge case gets tested, the training gap gets a fix, the job-fear gets named honestly and answered with real facts. This situation is different: if Denise's private intention and public statement genuinely conflict, there's no version of “name the concern and answer it honestly” that resolves it, because the honest answer to the preparers' fear would contradict what the sponsor has told them.

This is the point where the project, as currently framed, is not deliverable — not because of a technical gap, but because the political situation itself contains a contradiction the consultant can't design around. Recognizing this and naming it is a distinct skill from the rest of this module's techniques, and it's easy to miss, because the instinct is to keep trying harder versions of “surface the concern and address it,” when the actual problem is that addressing it honestly isn't currently possible given what's been said publicly.

contentSections.problem: Write the conversation with Denise that names this contradiction professionally, without accusing her of lying and without quietly going along with it.

steps.label: State the observation neutrally, without characterizing intent
steps.work: “I want to raise something directly. I've heard, separately, that reducing next season's seasonal headcount by two might be part of the longer-term thinking here — and I know the message to the preparer team has been that this isn't about replacing anyone. I want to check where things actually stand, because those two things pointed in different directions is something I'd want to know about before it becomes a bigger problem.”
steps.why: Stating the observation as a fact to be checked, rather than an accusation, gives Denise room to clarify, correct, or confirm without being immediately put on the defensive — which is what actually gets an honest answer instead of a defensive one.

steps.label: Name what happens if the contradiction is real and unaddressed
steps.work: “If that private plan is real and the public message stays as-is, I don't think I can keep working with the preparer team in good faith — they specifically asked, and were told directly that this wasn't about their jobs.”
steps.why: This states a genuine professional limit clearly, rather than either quietly going along with the contradiction or unilaterally deciding to blow it up — it gives Denise the actual stakes before any decision is forced.

steps.label: Offer the range of options rather than issuing an ultimatum
steps.work: “There are a few honest ways forward from here: the headcount plan isn't actually decided and the public message can stay accurate as it is; or it is a real plan, and the message to the team needs to change to something true, even if that's a harder conversation; or, if neither of those is workable, I'd need to step back from this engagement rather than keep representing something I now know isn't accurate.”
steps.why: Presenting real options, including the option of the consultant stepping back, treats this as a genuine decision point for Denise rather than a threat — and it's honest about what the consultant will and won't do depending on her answer.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure, different situation. A different client's engineering director privately tells you the automation project is really meant to build a case for outsourcing the whole department within a year, while publicly the project is framed to the department as “making everyone's job easier.” Apply the same three-step structure.

blanks.prompt: State the observation neutrally.
blanks.answer: Something like: 'I want to check something — I've heard the longer-term thinking here may include using this project's results to support an outsourcing case, and the message to the department has been that this is purely about making the job easier. I want to understand where things actually stand before I keep building something that gets used that way without anyone on the team knowing.'
accept: neutrally states the apparent contradiction as something to verify, not an accusation
blanks.why: The same neutral framing works here — stating the observation as a fact to check gives the director room to clarify without being cornered.

blanks.prompt: Name what happens if it's real and unaddressed.
blanks.answer: Something like: 'If that's accurate and the message to the department doesn't change, I'm not comfortable continuing to build something the team believes is for a different purpose than it actually is.'
accept: states a genuine professional limit about continuing to build something under a misleading public framing
blanks.why: This names the real stake honestly, the same way the Corrigan version did, without yet deciding the outcome unilaterally.

blanks.prompt: Offer the range of options.
blanks.answer: Something like: 'A few ways forward: the outsourcing consideration isn't actually decided and the current message stays accurate; or it is a real direction, and the department needs a true, if harder, message about it; or if neither works, I'd need to step back from the engagement.'
accept: offers a real range of honest paths forward, including stepping back, rather than an ultimatum
blanks.why: The same three-option structure — nothing changed, an honest reframe, or stepping back — gives the client a genuine decision rather than forcing one particular outcome.

faded.procedure: When a political contradiction, not a technical gap, makes a project undeliverable as framed: state the observation neutrally as something to verify, name the real professional limit if it's confirmed and unaddressed, and offer the genuine range of options — including stepping back — rather than either forcing ahead or quietly going along with it.

contentSections.body: Not every problem in this module is solvable by surfacing and addressing a concern — sometimes the honest finding is that the project, as currently framed, can't be delivered. Naming that professionally, with real options, is a consulting skill in its own right.

History, technology, pricing, competitors

Because clients are always reassured by hearing a specific number, regardless of context
It doesn't — a vague reassurance is always the safer choice

questions.from: Previous module — Explaining AI to People Who Don't Care How It Works

Dismiss the article as irrelevant
Concede and compress the timeline to match the room's enthusiasm

It doesn't risk anything as long as the speaker's tone is confident

Length — a longer exclusions section is always more useful
Legal language — exclusions only work if phrased formally

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Acceptance: what "done" means, agreed in writing
description: "Done" is a feeling until it's a checklist — acceptance criteria written against the original scope, agreed before final sign-off, are what keep the end of an engagement from becoming its own dispute.

learningObjectives.text: Convert a scope document's deliverables into specific, checkable acceptance criteria agreed before final sign-off

contentSections.body: Six months after the March kickoff, the extraction pipeline is live, Walt's edge cases are handled, the preparer team's concerns got a real answer, and the rollout is genuinely working. Priya asks the natural next question: “so — are we done? Can we close this out?” It's a harder question than it sounds, because “done” was never actually defined anywhere as a specific, checkable thing — the scope document names deliverables, but nobody wrote down what it means for each one to count as finished.

“Done” left as a feeling invites exactly the same kind of dispute this whole phase has been built to prevent — someone remembers the bar differently than someone else, at the exact moment (closing) when both sides most want a clean, mutually agreed ending. Acceptance criteria fix this by converting the scope document's deliverables into specific, checkable statements, agreed in writing before final sign-off: not “the extraction pipeline is built,” but “the pipeline correctly extracts fields from the document types in the discovery-phase inventory at the accuracy level shown in the pilot, has been handed over with a written runbook, and staff have completed the one included training session.”

This isn't a new document from scratch — it's largely the original scope document's deliverables and exclusions, restated as pass/fail statements both sides can check against the actual, finished thing rather than against memory or a general sense of satisfaction. Writing it down before sign-off, not after a disagreement starts, is what makes “are we done” a checklist instead of a negotiation.

contentSections.problem: Convert Corrigan's core scope deliverable — the document-intake extraction pipeline — into specific, checkable acceptance criteria.

steps.label: State the criterion against the pilot's measured result, not a vague standard
steps.work: “The pipeline correctly extracts fields from W-2s, 1099s, and standard receipts at or above the 91% no-fix-needed rate measured in the pilot, verified against a fresh sample of at least 20 production documents.”
steps.why: Tying the criterion to the pilot's actual number, checked against a fresh sample rather than the same pilot data, is what makes 'accurate enough' a testable fact instead of an opinion.

steps.label: State the criterion for the documented exclusions and limits
steps.work: “Documents outside the discovery-phase inventory (e.g. handwritten receipts, non-standard formats) are correctly flagged for manual entry, not silently guessed at, verified against at least 3 examples of each excluded type.”
steps.why: The exclusions list from earlier in this phase becomes its own checkable criterion — proving the boundary is respected, not just that the core feature works.

steps.label: State the criterion for handover artefacts
steps.work: “A written runbook exists covering how to check flagged items, how to add a new document format, and who to contact for support; staff training has been completed by everyone on the intake team as of the sign-off date.”
steps.why: Handover deliverables are just as real a part of 'done' as the technical build, and stating them as checkable facts prevents 'we'll get to documentation eventually' from quietly becoming permanent.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. Corrigan's scope also included the format-inventory discovery phase itself as a deliverable, from an earlier module. Write its acceptance criteria.

blanks.prompt: State the criterion for the discovery phase's core output.
blanks.answer: A written document-format inventory exists, covering at least 40-60 real client documents from the last filing season, categorized by type and edge case, as originally scoped
accept: a written inventory of the sampled documents exists, categorized by type, matching the original scope
blanks.why: This restates the original scope's specific numbers (40-60 documents) as a checkable fact rather than a vague 'the inventory is done.'

blanks.prompt: State a criterion tied to how the inventory was actually used.
blanks.answer: The build phase's fixed price and document-type coverage trace back to this inventory, with any type not in it correctly treated as an exclusion
accept: the later build phase's scope and pricing are shown to be grounded in the inventory's actual findings
blanks.why: This checks that the discovery phase did its actual job — grounding the fixed price in real data — not just that a document was produced and filed away unused.

faded.procedure: For every scoped deliverable, write a criterion that's checkable against a fresh, specific test — a real number, a real artefact, a real completed action — rather than a restatement of the deliverable's name. 'It exists' and 'it's done' aren't checkable; 'it covers these specific documents at this specific rate, verified against a fresh sample' is.

contentSections.scenario: You're proposing acceptance criteria to Priya and Denise before final sign-off, rather than after Priya's “are we done” question forces an improvised answer.
contentSections.question: Select every reason agreeing acceptance criteria in advance, rather than improvising an answer to “are we done,” actually matters.

items.label: It prevents the bar for “done” from being invented on the spot, under time pressure, by whoever happens to be asked first
It gives both sides the same checklist to verify against, instead of each side checking against their own memory of the scope
It gives the final invoice and sign-off a clear, agreed trigger, rather than an ambiguous sense that things feel finished
It makes the project look more impressive by listing out every deliverable formally

explanation.avoids-improvised-standard: Applicable. Deciding what counts as done in the moment, under the pressure of an actual question, tends to produce a lower or higher bar than either side would have agreed to calmly in advance.
explanation.shared-checklist: Applicable. A written, agreed checklist replaces two potentially different memories of the scope with one shared reference — the same value a kickoff recap provided earlier in this phase.
explanation.protects-final-invoice: Applicable. Final payment tied to a vague feeling of completeness is a recipe for a stalled or disputed final invoice — a specific, agreed trigger avoids that entirely.
explanation.makes-project-look-bigger: Not applicable — the goal of acceptance criteria is clarity and verifiability, not the appearance of scale, and treating it as a scale-signaling exercise misses its actual purpose.

contentSections.synthesis: Acceptance criteria agreed before sign-off replace an improvised, memory-dependent judgment call with a shared, checkable standard — exactly the same shift from “trust me, it's fine” to “here's what we agreed, verified” that this whole phase has been building toward since the very first scope document.

contentSections.body: “Done” left undefined invites a dispute at exactly the moment both sides most want a clean ending. Convert the scope's deliverables into specific, checkable acceptance criteria, and agree them before sign-off, not after.

title: The final report nobody has to be walked through
description: A final report that only makes sense with the consultant sitting next to the reader explaining it isn't actually finished — it needs to stand on its own for someone reading it cold, months from now.

learningObjectives.text: Structure a final report so it's self-explanatory to a reader with no memory of the engagement's history
State real numbers and named limitations plainly rather than in vague, reassuring language

contentSections.title: The report that needs a narrator

contentSections.body: A junior colleague drafts Corrigan's final report as a set of bullet points that made complete sense in the meeting where they were presented, walked through slide by slide: “Phase 1 complete. Phase 2 numbers strong. Walt's concerns addressed. Rollout successful.” A year from now, when Corrigan brings in a different consultant to extend the system, or when a new partner joins and wants to understand what was actually delivered, none of these bullet points mean anything without the same person standing next to them explaining what each one refers to.

A final report has a different job than a status update or a kickoff recap — those are read close to the events they describe, by people who were mostly there. A final report is read cold, potentially much later, by people who weren't in any of the rooms this phase has described. It needs the same self-contained quality lesson 4 of the previous module taught for an email that might get forwarded, applied to an entire document.

A report that holds up on its own states, in plain language, without requiring a narrator: **what was actually done** (the specific deliverables, not “Phase 1 complete”); **what it achieved, with real numbers** (91% no-fix-needed on standard documents, not “strong results”); **what's explicitly not included or still a known limitation** (handwritten receipts still routed to manual review, not silently omitted); **who owns it now and what happens next** (Priya owns day-to-day operation, referring to the runbook; the 30-day monitoring window closes on a specific date). Each of these is a plain, complete sentence a stranger could read and understand without asking a follow-up question.

contentSections.title: Rewriting the bullet points into a real report

contentSections.code:
Draft final report to Corrigan (junior colleague's version):

"Phase 1 complete. Phase 2 numbers strong. Walt's concerns addressed. Rollout successful."
contentSections.question: What's the actual, structural flaw here, beyond just being short?

options.label: Every line depends on shared context from meetings the reader may not have attended and refers to nothing specific enough to verify — “strong,” “addressed,” and “successful” are all unstated, uncheckable judgments
The report should have more phases listed for completeness
The report shouldn't mention Walt by name at all

feedback.unverifiable-shorthand: Correct. None of these four lines can be checked against anything specific — a reader with no memory of the engagement has no way to know what “strong” means numerically, what “addressed” actually changed, or what “successful” is being measured against.
feedback.not-enough-phases: The number of phases listed isn't the actual problem — even a longer list of equally vague phase names would carry the same flaw.
feedback.shouldnt-name-walt: Naming Walt's specific, real contribution (finding the out-of-state-rental case) is actually valuable, specific information for the report — the problem is that this draft doesn't even attempt that, it just gestures at 'concerns addressed' with no content behind it.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A report built from meeting-shorthand reads as complete to whoever sat through the meetings it summarizes and as nearly meaningless to anyone else. The fix isn't a longer list of the same kind of phrase — it's replacing each vague judgment with the specific fact behind it: the real number, the real finding, the real remaining limitation.

contentSections.body: A final report is read cold, later, by people who weren't in the room. State what was done, what it achieved with real numbers, what's still a known limitation, and who owns it now — in complete, specific sentences that don't need a narrator.

title: Handing over ownership properly
description: An automation only the consultant understands is a liability the day the consultant leaves — real handover means a named internal owner with real documentation and real access, not a system that quietly keeps depending on the person who built it.

learningObjectives.text: Identify what a genuine handover of ownership requires beyond a document being written

contentSections.title: Documentation that isn't actually a handover

contentSections.body: The runbook exists — twelve pages, covering how to check flagged items and how to add a new document format. Three months after the engagement closes, a document type genuinely does need adding, and Priya emails: “can you walk us through this? We have the runbook but nobody's actually done this before.” The document existing didn't, on its own, transfer the ability to use it — that's a different, harder thing than writing twelve pages and calling it done.

A genuine handover has three parts, and a runbook alone only covers one of them. **A named owner** — not “the team” or “whoever's available,” but a specific person (Priya) whose job it now explicitly includes understanding and maintaining this system. **Real documentation**, which the runbook provides — but documentation is necessary, not sufficient. **Demonstrated capability** — the named owner has actually done the key maintenance tasks at least once, with the consultant present to catch what the document didn't explain clearly enough, before the consultant is gone and it's the only reference left.

Skipping the third part is the most common way a handover looks complete and isn't. A document written by someone who deeply understands the system often has exactly the gaps someone with that understanding wouldn't notice — the steps that feel too obvious to write down. The only way to catch those gaps is watching someone who doesn't already know the system try to follow the document and use it for real, while there's still time to fix what's missing.

contentSections.problem: Design the real handover for Corrigan's document-intake pipeline, beyond the twelve-page runbook.

steps.label: Name the specific owner, explicitly
steps.work: Priya Chandra, director of operations, is named in writing as the pipeline's owner — responsible for day-to-day operation, first point of contact for issues, and the person who decides when a new document format needs adding.
steps.why: Naming a specific person, in writing, is what prevents 'the team owns it' from quietly meaning nobody owns it once the consultant is gone.

steps.label: Schedule a supervised run-through of the key maintenance task before handover is considered complete
steps.work: Before the engagement closes, Priya walks through adding a new (test) document format herself, using only the runbook, with the consultant present only to observe and note where she got stuck or asked a question the document didn't answer.
steps.why: This is the step that actually tests whether the documentation works, rather than assuming it does because the person who wrote it can follow it easily.

steps.label: Revise the runbook based on what the run-through actually revealed
steps.work: If Priya got stuck on, say, where confidence thresholds are configured, that section of the runbook gets rewritten before handover is signed off — not noted as a future improvement.
steps.why: The gaps found in the supervised run-through are exactly the gaps that would otherwise surface for the first time after the consultant is gone, at the worst possible moment to discover them.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. Design the handover for the checking-flagged-items task — the day-to-day work of reviewing items the pipeline routed for manual review.

blanks.prompt: Who should be named as owner of this specific task, and why might it be a different person than the pipeline's overall owner?
blanks.answer: Walt Sorensen, since he's the one actually reviewing flagged items day to day — the overall system owner (Priya) and the day-to-day task owner (Walt) can reasonably be different people, as long as both are named explicitly
accept: Walt, as the person who actually does this task daily, distinct from Priya as overall system owner
blanks.why: A handover doesn't need a single owner for everything — it needs every task to have a named owner, which can legitimately be different people for different tasks.

blanks.prompt: What would the supervised run-through look like for this task?
blanks.answer: Walt reviews a batch of real flagged items using only the documented process, with the consultant observing where the documented workflow doesn't match what he actually needs to decide (e.g. what information he needs to see to make the call)
accept: Walt does the flagged-item review himself, using only the documentation, while being observed for gaps
blanks.why: Same logic as the format-adding task — the only real test of whether the documentation supports the actual task is watching the actual owner do the actual task with it.

faded.procedure: For every distinct maintenance or operational task in the handover: name a specific owner (who may differ by task), have them perform the task using only the documentation while being observed, and revise the documentation based on exactly what that observation revealed — before considering the handover complete.

contentSections.title: What a shadow dependency actually costs

contentSections.body: A handover isn't complete when the document is written — it's complete when the named owner has actually done the task themselves, using only the document, with the gaps that revealed already fixed.

title: The follow-up that catches the drift
description: A system that was working at handover doesn't stay working by default — habits revert, edge cases accumulate, and a scheduled proactive check-in catches drift while it's still small, instead of waiting for a support call once it's already a problem.

learningObjectives.text: Design a proactive follow-up check-in that checks for specific, plausible drift rather than a generic status update

contentSections.body: At handover, everything checked out: Priya could add a format, Walt could review flagged items confidently, the acceptance criteria all passed. Four months later, next tax season's crunch hits, a new seasonal preparer joins who never got the original training, and — nobody notices for three weeks — Walt has quietly gone back to double-checking every return by hand, not because anything's actually broken, but because a new person's uncertainty made the whole team more cautious by default. Nothing failed. Something drifted, silently, and nobody was watching for it because there was no support ticket to notice.

A system passing its acceptance criteria at handover is a snapshot, not a guarantee. People forget training, staff turn over, informal habits creep back under pressure, and none of that shows up as a broken feature — it shows up as slow, quiet disuse that looks, from a distance, like everything is fine, because nothing has technically stopped working.

Waiting for a support call to catch this only works for problems that announce themselves loudly. Drift doesn't announce itself; it accumulates. The fix is a scheduled, proactive follow-up — typically at 30, 60, and 90 days after handover — that specifically checks for the plausible drift risks named at handover time, not a generic “how's it going?” email that's easy to answer with a reflexive “good, thanks” regardless of what's actually happening.

contentSections.scenario: In similar automation rollouts, when a new staff member joins without the original training and nobody proactively checks in, roughly what share of a previously well-adopted workflow reverts to old manual habits within about two months, based on typical patterns.
contentSections.question: Estimate: in cases like this, what share of the previously smooth workflow tends to revert, at least partially, to old manual habits within roughly two months of an untrained new hire joining, absent any proactive check-in?
contentSections.explanation: Estimates vary by context, but a substantial share — often somewhere around a third to half — commonly reverts at least partially, because a new team member's uncertainty tends to make everyone around them more cautious by default, and nobody official is watching for it. The exact number matters less than the mechanism: drift compounds quietly and is rarely reported as a problem, since nothing is technically broken — which is exactly why a scheduled, proactive check-in (rather than waiting for a complaint) is the only reliable way to catch it early.

contentSections.title: Designing a check-in that actually checks something

contentSections.scenario: Designing the 30/60/90-day follow-up for Corrigan, given the specific drift risks already named at handover: new-hire training gaps, and Walt's habit of full manual double-checking.
contentSections.question: Select every element that makes this a genuinely useful proactive check-in, rather than a generic status email.

items.label: “Has anyone joined the intake team since handover, and have they completed the training session?”
“Is Walt still reviewing every return in full, or is he trusting the flagged-item queue for the rest?” — checked with Priya or observed directly, not just asked of Walt himself
A quick check of the actual flagged-item volume against the pilot's expected rate, to catch a silent accuracy drop
“Just checking in — how's everything going?”

explanation.specific-question-training: Applicable. This directly checks the specific drift risk named at handover — a new hire missing training — rather than hoping it comes up unprompted.
explanation.specific-question-walt: Applicable. Asking about Walt's actual behavior, and checking it against what Priya observes rather than only Walt's own self-report, is what catches a habit reverting quietly rather than relying on Walt to volunteer it.
explanation.specific-metric: Applicable. A real number checked against the pilot's baseline can catch an accuracy problem before anyone notices it subjectively — the same value a measured baseline provided back in the pricing module.
explanation.generic-check-in: Not applicable. A generic “how's it going” is easy to answer reflexively without actually checking anything, and it doesn't test any of the specific risks known to be plausible here.

contentSections.synthesis: A follow-up that catches drift asks specific, named questions tied to specific, plausible risks identified at handover — not a general temperature check that's easy to answer without actually looking.

contentSections.body: A system working at handover is a snapshot, not a guarantee — habits and training gaps drift quietly without ever looking like a broken feature. A scheduled, specific, proactive check-in catches that drift while it's still small.

title: Turning one engagement into a reference
description: Asking for a reference at the moment genuine value has just been delivered and confirmed, tied to something specific, gets a real answer — asking generically, or at the wrong moment, reads as self-interested and usually gets a polite non-answer.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the right moment and specific framing to ask for a reference, tied to confirmed, delivered value

contentSections.title: Why timing and specificity both matter

contentSections.body: The 90-day follow-up lands well: no drift found, the training gap from the new hire got caught and fixed at the 30-day check-in before it became a habit, and Denise says, unprompted, “honestly, this has been one of the smoother projects we've run.” This is close to the best possible moment to ask for a reference — not because it's convenient timing for the consultant, but because it's the moment where genuine, confirmed value is freshest and most specific in Denise's mind.

A reference request generically timed — sent in a template email weeks after the engagement closed, with no specific tie to a result — reads as a favor being asked, disconnected from anything Denise is actually thinking about at that moment, and tends to get a polite, low-effort response or no response at all. A request made right after a specific, confirmed win, referencing that exact thing, reads completely differently, because it's asking Denise to describe something she was already, genuinely thinking about a moment before.

The request itself should be as specific as the win it follows: not “would you be willing to serve as a reference,” but “would you be open to a short call with a prospective client about specifically how the discovery-phase approach worked for the format inventory — that's often the part people are most skeptical of going in.” A specific ask, tied to a specific, real result, is both easier to say yes to and more useful when someone actually does it, because it produces a concrete story instead of a generic compliment.

contentSections.title: The ask that follows the moment

contentSections.problem: Write the reference-request message to Denise, right after her unprompted “one of the smoother projects” comment at the 90-day check-in.

steps.label: Acknowledge what she just said, specifically
steps.work: “That means a lot to hear, especially given how much was genuinely uncertain going in — thank you.”
steps.why: Responding to the specific thing she said, rather than pivoting immediately to the ask, keeps the moment feeling like a real conversation rather than a transaction.

steps.label: Make a specific, low-friction ask tied to a specific result
steps.work: “If it's ever useful, I'd love to be able to point a prospective client to you for a short call about specifically how the discovery-phase approach worked here — that's usually the part people are most skeptical of before they've seen it work.”
steps.why: Naming the exact topic (the discovery phase) rather than a vague 'say good things about us' gives Denise something concrete and easy to actually talk about if she says yes.

steps.label: Make it easy to decline or defer without awkwardness
steps.work: “No pressure at all if that's not something you're up for — just wanted to ask while it was on both our minds.”
steps.why: An easy, pressure-free exit is what keeps the request itself from damaging the relationship if the answer is no or not right now — which matters more than any single reference.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. Solano Behavioral Health Group's founder, Dr. Ibarra, emails three weeks after her own engagement's follow-up: “the therapists have genuinely stopped complaining about note-writing time — that alone was worth it.” Write the reference-request message.

blanks.prompt: Acknowledge what she said, specifically.
blanks.answer: Something like: 'That's genuinely great to hear — the note-writing time was exactly the pain point we were trying to solve, so I'm glad it's actually landed that way in practice.'
accept: a specific acknowledgment referencing the exact thing she praised (note-writing time)
blanks.why: Same reasoning as the Corrigan case — responding specifically to what she said keeps this a real conversation, not an immediate pivot to asking for something.

blanks.prompt: Make a specific, low-friction ask tied to this exact result.
blanks.answer: Something like: 'If it's ever useful, I'd love to point another practice considering this to you for a short conversation about the note-writing time change specifically — that's usually the thing clinicians are most skeptical will actually happen.'
accept: asks for a reference specifically about the note-writing time improvement, not a generic testimonial
blanks.why: Tying the ask to the exact, specific win she just named (rather than a general 'would you recommend us') keeps the request concrete and easy to say yes to.

faded.procedure: When a client volunteers a specific, genuine piece of praise: acknowledge it specifically, ask for a specific and low-friction reference tied to that exact result, and make declining easy — the specificity of both the trigger and the ask is what makes this work, not the act of asking itself.

contentSections.body: A reference asked for generically, disconnected from a specific moment, gets a generic non-answer. Ask right after a specific, confirmed win, tied to exactly that result, with an easy way to say no.

title: Practice — Write Acceptance Criteria for Seven Deliverables
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given a deliverable or closing scenario, apply this module's acceptance, reporting, handover, and follow-up skills.

learningObjectives.text: Write specific, checkable acceptance criteria for a range of deliverables
Identify gaps in draft final reports, handovers, and follow-up plans

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing is timed, and the set doesn't expire — do all seven now or split them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the lab — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Write a Closing Report for a Completed Engagement
description: Write the full closing report for Solano Behavioral Health Group's session-note project: what was done, what it achieved, what's still open, and who owns it now.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a closing report that stands on its own for a reader with no history with the engagement
State real numbers, named limitations, and clear ownership rather than vague, reassuring summaries

contentSections.body: Solano Behavioral Health Group's session-note drafting tool has been live for four months. This lab writes the full closing report — the deliverable this entire phase has been building toward, applied one more time, to a different client, without a worked example to copy from directly.

contentSections.title: Solano's closing report
contentSections.brief: Using this module's structure, write the complete closing report for Solano's engagement. You'll need to invent plausible specifics (a pilot accuracy figure, named document/note types covered, a specific limitation, a named owner) consistent with the project described earlier in this phase — a tool that drafts a first-pass session note from a therapist's spoken summary, always reviewed before finalizing.
contentSections.deliverable: A closing report covering: what was done, what it achieved (with invented but plausible real numbers), what's explicitly still open or excluded, who owns it now, and acceptance criteria that were used to confirm 'done.'

stages.title: Write the acceptance criteria that were used to confirm 'done'
stages.instructions: Write at least 3 specific, checkable acceptance criteria for this project (e.g. an accuracy figure verified against a fresh sample, a handover artefact, a training completion), the way this module's lessons modeled for Corrigan.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least 3 specific, checkable criteria, each tied to a real, invented but plausible number or artefact.

stages.title: Write the 'what was done' and 'what it achieved' sections
stages.instructions: Write these sections so a reader with zero history with the project understands exactly what was built and what real numbers resulted — no unexplained shorthand, following the previous module's forwarding-email standard.
stages.checkpoint: Every claim in these two sections would make sense to a stranger with no other context.

stages.title: Write the 'still open' and 'ownership' sections
stages.instructions: Name at least one specific, honest limitation (something explicitly out of scope or not yet fully solved) and name a specific internal owner with what they're responsible for.
stages.checkpoint: At least one specific limitation and one named owner with specific responsibilities are stated.

stages.title: Write the follow-up plan
stages.instructions: Write a 30/60/90-day follow-up plan with at least one specific, named drift risk to check at each interval — not a generic 'we'll check in.'
stages.checkpoint: Each of the three intervals has a specific, named thing being checked, not a generic status question.

rubric.criterion: Acceptance criteria are specific and checkable
rubric.meets: Each criterion names a real number, artefact, or completed action — not a restatement of the deliverable's name.

rubric.criterion: The report holds up for a reader with zero history
rubric.meets: No sentence depends on the reader having attended a meeting or conversation not described in the report itself.

rubric.criterion: Real numbers are stated plainly, not replaced with vague adjectives
rubric.meets: At least one specific measured or invented-but-plausible figure appears, tied to what it measures.

rubric.criterion: At least one honest limitation is named
rubric.meets: The report states something explicitly not covered or not yet fully solved, not just successes.

rubric.criterion: Ownership is specific, not generic
rubric.meets: A named person (not 'the team') is tied to specific ongoing responsibilities.

rubric.criterion: The follow-up plan checks specific, plausible risks
rubric.meets: Each of the three intervals names a concrete thing being checked, connected to a risk raised elsewhere in the report.

contentSections.body: A closing report is the last artefact of the engagement and often the only one anyone reads again — it earns that role by standing on its own, stating real numbers and real limits, and naming who's actually responsible for what happens next.

title: Checkpoint — Delivering and Closing
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous module, two from three modules back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's acceptance, reporting, and handover distinctions, and earlier modules' resistance and explanation distinctions, without looking them up

questions.from: This module — Delivering and Closing
questions.prompt: Priya asks “are we done?” with no acceptance criteria previously agreed. What's the risk in answering that question improvised, on the spot?

options.label: The bar for “done” gets invented under time pressure, by whoever happens to be asked first, instead of reflecting a standard both sides actually agreed to
There's no real risk, since both sides know the project well by that point
The only risk is that it takes longer to answer than a quick yes or no

questions.explanation: An improvised answer under pressure tends to set a bar neither side would have calmly agreed to in advance — the same reasoning that made written kickoff recaps and proactive scoping valuable earlier in this phase.

questions.from: This module — Delivering and Closing
questions.prompt: What makes an acceptance criterion actually checkable, rather than a restatement of the deliverable's name?

options.label: It names a specific, fresh test — a real number, artefact, or completed action verified against new evidence, not just the deliverable's existence
Its length — a longer criterion is always more checkable
Whether it's phrased using formal contract language

questions.explanation: “The pipeline is built” isn't checkable; “correctly extracts fields at or above 91% on a fresh sample” is — specificity and a fresh test are what make a criterion actually verifiable.

questions.from: This module — Delivering and Closing
questions.prompt: Why does a final report built from meeting-shorthand (“Phase 1 complete,” “concerns addressed”) fail for its actual audience?

options.label: It's read cold, later, by people who weren't in the meetings it summarizes, and none of its claims are specific enough to verify without that missing context
It's too long for anyone to read
It doesn't fail — this level of detail is appropriate for a final report

questions.explanation: A final report's real audience often isn't the people who sat through the engagement — it's read later, cold, by people with no memory of the meetings the shorthand refers to.

questions.from: This module — Delivering and Closing
questions.prompt: Why doesn't a written runbook, on its own, count as a completed handover?

options.label: Documentation written by someone who deeply understands the system often has gaps — the steps that feel too obvious to write down — that only surface when someone else actually tries to use it
Runbooks are never useful for anything
A handover is complete the moment any document exists, regardless of whether anyone has used it

questions.explanation: A handover needs a named owner who has demonstrated the task using only the documentation, because the author's own understanding hides exactly the gaps a first-time user would hit.

questions.from: Previous module — People, Politics and Resistance
questions.prompt: Walt quietly avoids using the new pipeline without formally objecting. What's the more useful way to read this?

options.label: As information worth investigating — he likely has specific knowledge about a real risk the system doesn't yet account for
As a personality trait to route around by driving adoption elsewhere
As a formal objection requiring immediate escalation

questions.explanation: Resistance is usually information — investigating it surfaced a real, previously untested case type.

questions.from: Previous module — People, Politics and Resistance
questions.prompt: Why doesn't a vague, unprompted reassurance like “don't worry about your jobs” actually resolve unspoken job-loss fear?

options.label: It has nothing specific to check against, and can even read as confirmation the concern is real enough to need addressing
It resolves the fear completely if said with confidence
Job-related reassurance is never appropriate from a consultant

questions.explanation: A vague, unprompted reassurance with no specific content can backfire by making the concern seem more credible, not less.

questions.from: Previous module — People, Politics and Resistance
questions.prompt: What made Denise's private headcount intention categorically different from Walt's resistance or the preparers' earlier unspoken fear?

options.label: It contained an actual contradiction between a private intention and a public statement, which honest engagement alone couldn't resolve
It wasn't actually different — the same techniques resolved it identically
It was different only because Denise is the sponsor

questions.explanation: The earlier situations had a true, honest answer available once surfaced; this one didn't, because honesty itself would contradict a specific prior public statement.

questions.from: Previous module — People, Politics and Resistance
questions.prompt: What's the actual goal of interviewing someone about a previous failed rollout?

options.label: Recovering specific, actionable institutional knowledge that exists nowhere else
Helping them process their feelings about it
Confirming the previous vendor was at fault

questions.explanation: The interview's purpose is extracting specific, testable design requirements from someone who lived through an undocumented failure.

questions.from: Three modules back — Explaining AI to People Who Don't Care How It Works
questions.prompt: Someone in the partners meeting asks if the pipeline is “basically like a really smart intern reading the documents.” What does that module say the analogy gets right and wrong?

options.label: It rightly conveys that the output is a first draft a person reviews, but wrongly implies ongoing, cumulative learning from correction and personal accountability, which a fixed model doesn't have between retraining cycles
It's entirely accurate and can be used without any qualification
It's entirely wrong and should never be used at all

questions.explanation: Every common AI analogy is half right — naming what it correctly conveys and what it wrongly implies, in the same breath, is what keeps it from quietly misleading the listener.

questions.from: Three modules back — Explaining AI to People Who Don't Care How It Works
questions.prompt: Denise asks to forward your capability-briefing email to partners who weren't at the kickoff. What does that module say to do?

options.label: Write it assuming it will be read by someone with none of the meeting's shared context — no unexplained shorthand, no assumed “as discussed”
Ask Denise not to forward it, since it wasn't written for a wider audience
Leave it as-is — once it's sent, who reads it isn't the writer's concern

questions.explanation: Once an email leaves the outbox, whether it stays with the original reader isn't the writer's decision anymore — writing for the forward means it holds up for whoever it actually reaches.

contentSections.body: This is the last checkpoint in the phase. What stuck across all five modules is what carries forward — the retrieval design doesn't stop mattering just because the phase is ending.
